articles.title: Tinned food and long-life milk boost retail sales after 'Be Ready' campaign launch
articles.standfirst: People stocking up on long-life food drove retail sales higher October, according to official data.
paragraphs: Retail sales rose in October, driven by people buying long-life food such as tinned goods and UHT milk, according to official figures.
Sales volumes were 0.7% higher as people responded to the government's emergency preparedness "Be Ready" campaign, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said.
The campaign encouraged people to stock up in case of disruption to essential services by severe weather or cyberattacks.
Separate research released last week suggested that while households were stockpiling essentials, they were not panic buying.
The government campaign encouraged people to keep three days-worth of food and water in their homes.
Wet wipes, a torch and cash were also recommended.
Data from retail research firm Worldpanel by Numerator indicated last week that  people were stocking up on items including tinned meat, bottled water and hand sanitiser.
The latest official sales figures from the ONS add to the evidence that the public has begun stockpiling.
"Supermarkets have told us that sales of long-life food items such as tinned food and UHT milk were boosted by the government's 'Be Ready' campaign," ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said.
"Meanwhile fuel sales have been recovering from earlier low levels, despite pump prices rising again."
The rise in retail sales last month beat some economists' expectations - they had predicted a slight fall - and the uptick came after a 0.6% decline in September.
As well as sales being boosted by people buying essentials, visits to art galleries and clothing purchases were also higher in October.
The boost in sales comes at the beginning of the festive period, which is normally the busiest time of the year for retailers.

Jacqui Baker, partner and head of retail at auditing firm RSM UK, said that "retailers will want to see out the year with some Christmas cheer before consumers batten down the hatches in the New Year as energy costs skyrocket and inflation ramps up further".
Typical energy bills are forecast to go up by £443 per year from January, pushing up the pace of price rises.
Separate economic data released on Friday showed the government borrowed slightly less than economists had expected in October.
Borrowing - the difference between public sector spending and income - was £17bn last month, the ONS said.
Although that was £0.8bn higher than October last year, it was below analysts' forecasts of about £18bn.
Interest repayments were £11.2bn - the highest October debt interest figure on record - and £2.8bn more than a year ago.
These repayments have been pushed up by higher inflation, as payments on index-linked government bonds are linked to the inflation rate.
Inflation rose to 3.6% in October, mainly because of higher petrol and diesel prices. The rate has been rising in recent months as the Iran war has driven up the cost of energy and fuel.

articles.title: Should AI be judging our credit worthiness?
articles.standfirst: Would AI be a good judge of whether you should get a mortgage, car loan or mobile phone contract?
paragraphs: Sophie Hope's credit score was hit by identity fraud
Getting approval for a mortgage, a car loan or even a mobile phone contract can rest on a credit score.
Sophie Hope was on the sharp end of just such a decision.

"When I first checked my credit score, it was excellent. But then my mortgage application was suddenly denied by the lender because of my credit report. It was a massive shock as I'd never had bad credit. When I looked into it, my score had gone to 'very poor'," she says.
It turns out, the Brighton-based nail technician and content creator, had been the victim of identity fraud.
"Someone had opened accounts in my name across various catalogue sites and ordered multiple items, including a PlayStation 4 and Nike socks," she says.

"Without me knowing, the debt was transferred to a secondary finance company. It spent three to four years accumulating in the background. It was only when I went to apply for a mortgage that I discovered how severely it had dragged down my credit score," she says.
Credit scores are "backward looking" says Funmi Olufunwa
Hope's experience shows how crucial a credit score can be, but, as in her case, it does not tell the full story.
"As a nation, we are overly obsessed with credit scores," says Funmi Olufunwa, a consumer finance lawyer and founder of financial education business, Hoops Finance.
Three firms - Experian, Equifax and TransUnion - produce credit scores in the UK, and they all work from roughly the same data.
"A credit score is backward looking. It's looking at what has happened in the past, which doesn't necessarily predict the future," says Olufunwa.
"But when somebody's looking to lend you money, they're looking at what actually is affordable," she says.
Traditional credit scoring systems also disadvantage "thin-file applicants" - young people and recent immigrants to the UK who won't have built up a credit history.
But with more financial data available than ever before - and a growing appetite for AI to make sense of it - could artificial intelligence help lenders work out who is safe to lend to?
In the US lending decisions will often hinge on a credit score from a company called FICO, which uses data from the big three credit assessment firms.
But AI-powered lending firms, Upstart and Zest AI have both built businesses which offer lenders an extra option when it comes to assessing a client's credit worthiness.

"Thanks to our machine-learning models that look at more than 2,500 variables, we believe we can make significantly more loans at low prices to borrowers from every demographic group," Upstart said in statement.

Mortgage expert and founder and CEO of The Mortgage Mum, Sarah Tucker says: "AI has the potential to help lenders analyse much broader sets of information, identify patterns more quickly and build a more individual picture of someone's affordability and risk."

If technology allows lenders to understand so-called thin-file applicants better, rather than simply applying increasingly rigid rules, Tucker believes there is "a real opportunity to improve financial inclusion".
But like with many other applications of AI into everyday life, there are concerns.
"Consumers need to understand what information is being used to make decisions about them, and they need to be able to challenge something when it is wrong," Tucker explains.
Credit scores have been a contentious topic for decades for this very reason, says Sandra Wachter, professor of Technology and Regulation at the University of Oxford.

"We are not assessing if past decisions were right," Wachter argues, adding, AI does not know about existing social inequalities that impact decisions and could just "replicate what it has seen in the past".
While companies like Upstart and Zest AI see technology as a tool for financial inclusion, Wachter believes that real transformation requires accountability, as well as automation.
She stresses that firms must apply existing regulations and establish new guardrails to ensure that AI does not simply perpetuate the biases of the past.
"Not putting any safeguards in place will fortify, foster, and enhance discrimination."
Upstart says it is tackling that issue.

"We've invested in creating objective, automated evaluations to identify bias, and we've incorporated those evaluations into our model training process so it evolves to become even more accurate and more fair over time," the company said in a statement.
Evangeline Atkinson (left) and Laura Mills co-founders of Noggin HQ
Evangeline Atkinson had a frustrating experience over her credit score.
"I was at university, paying rent, paying bills, as I had been doing for many years. I tried to get a £30-a-month phone contract, and they said no," she recalls.
"When I dug into it, it was because I was completely invisible to the system. No record could be found for me at any of the big three credit reference agencies."
That experience inspired her to try to change the system.
In 2021, Atkinson founded a credit reference agency with her best-friend from school, who had also experienced difficulties getting credit.
Their firm, Noggin HQ, was authorised by the FCA in June. Atkinson explains it was set up to help consumers access affordable credit by analysing their current account transactional data.
The platform helps lenders interpret thousands of individual data points about a person's spending habits.
Crucially, it does this without using AI, which Atkinson has also argued "carries the risk of inbuilt bias".
"You have to be very careful", she warns. "It's very sensitive data and it would be very easy for the models to be inferring various kind of protected characteristics."
Experian announced a partnership with OpenAI in August
Perhaps conscious of change, the big three credit scoring firms have all started experimenting with AI.

Experian announced a partnership with OpenAI in August 2026, letting users check their credit score inside ChatGPT. Equifax launched a platform called Equifax Amplify AI, which it says uses machine learning to sharpen credit assessment and fraud detection.
Meanwhile, in March TransUnion announced it was integrating Google's Gemini models "within its proprietary analytic data assets".
As for the future of credit scoring, companies are starting to look beyond traditional methods, according to consumer finance lawyer Funmi Olufunwa.
"They are beginning to realise that traditional credit scoring is inherently backward-looking, and that there are better predictors of the future out there."
Whether consumers will be happy with AI playing a part in working out their future credit ratings is another thing.
Any change might be led by the younger, tech-savvy generation.
"They feel comfortable with their data being used this way, simply because it's the world they've grown up in.
"I wonder if older cohorts, who may not use technology as much, will be quite as comfortable with it," says Olufunwa.

articles.title: Mouldy, infested housing for vulnerable people sold as ethical investments abroad
articles.standfirst: The properties are marketed at premium prices with claims of “government-backed” returns, the BBC finds.
paragraphs: Many of the companies marketing supported housing investments were linked to developer Lee Jones
"This building is hell on Earth," says Phil, describing the black mould and rats at Castleview House, the block of flats in Runcorn, Cheshire, where he lives.

But to an estate agent called Britské Reality - which translates as British Real Estate - working with investors hundreds of miles away in the Czech Republic, the flat Phil rents through his benefits was an exciting business opportunity.
The estate agent's marketing material said the flat was a government-funded source of income for investors, where tenants were taken care of and the property was in excellent condition.
A Czech investor bought it last year for £163,150, more than double the £75,000 cost of similar apartments in the block.

The BBC has found more than 40 companies marketing similar properties to individuals in the UK and abroad, as businesses seek to profit from a government system intended to provide housing and support for vulnerable people.
About a dozen of these companies work with a property developer called Lee Jones, whose company sold Phil's flat.

The homes they are selling to investors are advertised as supported accommodation, a type of housing for people with issues including mental health problems or drug abuse issues, as well as people fleeing domestic violence.
The BBC saw mould on ceilings and overflowing rubbish when we visited Castleview House

Providers offering what is known as supported exempt accommodation are allowed to charge the taxpayer more than the usual housing benefit cap, because they have higher running costs. Tenants are entitled to care, support and supervision - although how much support should be provided is not defined.

While there are legitimate providers helping people back into independent living, the BBC has previously reported on how some are exploiting the system by taking the higher housing benefit payments but failing to provide support.

Our latest investigation found companies marketing supported housing properties to people in Hong Kong, Macau, Nigeria, Turkey, the Netherlands, the UK and other countries as a "secure", "government-backed" investment.

We also found adverts made misleading promises about the quality of the accommodation and support, with tenants saying they were receiving little or no care, while we observed examples of poor quality, unsafe accommodation.
Housing charities and experts have told the BBC the sector has been transformed into a profit-generating machine at the expense of some tenants' safety, care, and dignity.

Labour MP Abena Oppong-Asare, who chairs the Housing Select Committee, said it was "outrageous" that supported housing properties were being marketed as investments "particularly where there's public funds involved".
The BBC's findings were "alarming" and showed a sector "open to abuse", she added.
Promotional materials such as this social media post advertise the homes as "Secure, Government-Backed Wealth"
Lee Jones's company The Investment Room converted Castleview House in 2019 from an office block into more than 200 residential flats, including the one where Phil now lives.

Then Jones partnered with Nurture Housing Association. His company granted Nurture a 25-year-lease on some of the flats, to provide housing for people on government benefits. Jones has a close business relationship with Nurture's chief executive Chris Smith, with the pair also acting as joint directors of other housing companies.

Jones then worked with estate agents, which marketed the housing to investors in the UK and overseas using the regular cashflow generated by the 25-year lease with Nurture and the promise of government funding to justify inflated prices.

Lee Jones and Nurture have repeated this with property developments across England, including in Doncaster, Rotherham, Stockton-on-Tees and Bradford. These type of properties are also in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland but are funded and regulated differently.

Because neither profit-making private companies nor individuals can act as supported housing providers themselves, co-operation between developers, investors and publicly funded providers has become common.

The Czech marketing material found by the BBC said Nurture provides housing for people with mental health issues who receive the "aftercare program pursuant to Section 117 of the Mental Health Act", meaning they have been sectioned and discharged from hospital with a detailed care plan.
But Phil says he has never been sectioned under the Mental Health Act.
He does have severe depression and anxiety, and he is currently out of work. But he says he has never had any support or care, or met anyone working for Nurture during his time at the flat.

"Whoever marketed this property, the way they've worded it is total dishonesty," says Phil. "If they're looking to make as much profit as they can, then they clearly have no plans to fix the issues in the building."
Marketing images appeared to show Castleview House as newly refurbished with bright white interiors

Phil had no idea the flat he rents had been sold to overseas investors in May 2025 until the BBC contacted him. But there were clues: bills addressed to someone called Jan Hála had been coming through the letterbox for months.

Lee Jones told us that the properties his companies provide are "good quality accommodation" and he has no responsibility for the communal areas of Castleview House since he sold the freehold in 2021. He denied his relationship with Chris Smith amounted to a conflict of interest, but did not respond to questions about his role in marketing the properties.
Jan Hála, the Czech investor who now owns Phil's flat, and the Britské Reality estate agency did not respond to requests for comment.

We spoke to several other people living in flats run by Nurture Housing Association in Castleview House who said they were in supported accommodation. They reported receiving little or no help from Nurture but were afraid to speak out publicly for fear of eviction and becoming homeless.

There is also evidence that marketing materials for investors buying flats in Castleview were misleading. Investors were told Nurture was providing "specialist supported housing" - a claim which is repeated on its website.
According to the Regulator of Social Housing, this would mean it was providing a high level of care, equivalent to living in a care home.
But Nurture had not been registered as a specialised supported housing provider, the regulator said, and its claim to be providing this was "shocking".

In a statement, Nurture acknowledged that Castleview House is managed under a "general housing management model" and does not form part of its supported housing portfolio. It said it provided supported housing elsewhere through partners which were registered providers.
It said the Czech advert found by the BBC related to "historic marketing material" produced by third parties.

However, the BBC has seen marketing material from several other agents selling flats in Castleview House to investors, which also claim that Nurture is providing supported housing to the residents on a 25-year lease.

Nurture said it is not directly involved with the companies marketing the properties. But it said: "We will be reviewing communications with relevant agents and reminding them of the importance of ensuring that any information relating to Nurture is accurate, transparent and does not create misunderstanding regarding the accommodation or services provided."
While there are doubts about what kind of housing Nurture has been providing, the BBC also found other flats sold to investors overseas with tenants who were in supported exempt accommodation.
The web of companies involved in providing this housing and cross-border ownership means it can be difficult for vulnerable tenants to get help when there are problems with properties.

"The way that the current system works is there's different levels of involvement by different organisations and companies and no-one is directly accountable," Abena Oppong-Asare, the housing committee chairwoman, told us.

Mo, who has mental health issues, was housed in a studio flat in Cricklewood, north London, after he became homeless. The converted house containing his flat was bought by Gemelli London 2 Limited, a company run by French nationals living in the Czech Republic, for £1.83m in January last year.
Mo (right) pictured with a friend who also lived in the same building, says his ceiling collapsed and was not fixed for months

He says his supported housing provider, Windrush Alliance, receives nearly £2,000 a month via Barnet Council for the flat. Mo says he receives £340 in universal credit for living expenses every month - but he is expected to pay Windrush a monthly £120 service charge out of that.
Last year his ceiling collapsed after a leak went unrepaired for more than a year and Mo was temporarily housed in another flat in the property.
Mo says his weekly visits from a Windrush support worker feel like a tick-box exercise and do not help him with the mental health issues which have been keeping him out of work.

Gemelli's director Stephane Boussier told the BBC that when the company bought the property "no complaints from residents were disclosed". It was made aware of issues in August 2025, he said, and since then has "raised them with Windrush in writing, inspected the property and pressed for them to be resolved".
He added that Gemelli London 2 Limited receives about £1,365 per flat per month from Windrush and does not receive any of the extra housing benefit that would be used for vulnerable tenants.

Windrush said it was aware of issues at Mo's property and was "working with the building owner to put them right". According to Gemelli, the ceiling was repaired after the BBC contacted the two companies.
Windrush has previously been criticised by the Regulator for Social Housing for a "failure to meet the standards" of the regulator, including failing to ensure "tenants are safe in their homes".

It acknowledged that it "fell short in the past". It wrote off £1.8m in "funds to former directors and companies under their control", saying the company's financial position had been "compromised" by their actions. The company now has a new board in place.
Windrush told us its "priority is residents, not investors" and the rates it charges "are agreed with the relevant local authorities" and "any surplus is reinvested in our homes and services".
In Bradford, the BBC visited City Exchange and Colonnade House, two former office blocks which Lee Jones has converted into housing - with Nurture Housing Association managing many of the flats.
Many of the properties there were advertised as supported housing investments. Residents showed us cockroach infestations, faulty fire alarms, broken lifts, leaks through the ceiling and black mould.
Nurture Housing said it was only responsible for the individual homes that it manages and does not manage communal areas or "wider building infrastructure".
"Nurture Housing and its managing agents regularly raise these concerns with the block manager," the company said.

The freeholder for Phil's block, Castleview House, and City Exchange, blamed "defects" by the developer Lee Jones for the problems with the buildings and said it was taking legal action. Colonnade House has had several building management companies in recent years and the latest said it was addressing the problems.
None of these companies or individuals are breaking the law, but critics say they are exploiting a lack of regulation in the sector.

Three years after the Supported Housing Act was passed in England, which would put in place a licensing regime for supported housing providers and give local councils more powers to shut down providers that failed to meet the standards, it still has not been implemented.
"It's taken too long," said Jasmine Basran, head of policy and campaigns at housing charity Crisis. "In the meantime, this an area where we've seen the worst kind of exploitation."
Additional reporting by Lorna Acquah and Abi Smitton

articles.title: Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in stock market debut
articles.standfirst: Anthropic is the first purely AI company to be publicly listed, creating a test for the entire industry.
paragraphs: This video can not be played
Watch: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold?
Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion (£1.34 trillion).
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.
Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 each, showing there was plenty of excitement around AI.
Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?

In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.53, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day as the shares closed at $97.17.
Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet, which was down by 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%.

The buildout happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.
The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble.
"Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."
Anthropic has made one of the fastest trips from start up to IPO in history
While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever.
The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet more quickly.
It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude.

As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.
The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year.
That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion.
Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since.
Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.
But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.

With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market.
"There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said.
So, as individual investors and even researchers and investors at large funds ask themselves if Anthropic is really worth more than $1.7 trillion, or even more, there will be few answers available.
"We'll have a stab at it," Wilson said. "I don't think anyone really knows."
A few things will likely impact the company's success on the stock market in the near-term.

One of those things is the prospect of new laws governing the use of AI tools. In the US, where Anthropic is based, Democrats will be in many more positions of power come 2027, and several politicians have already said they will be looking to ensure AI tools are safe and have some guardrails attached.

Such regulation is currently unlikely at the federal level. US President Donald Trump on Thursday spoke about AI during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, alongside Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
Trump reiterated his position against "any form of robust regulation" around the technology, adding, "we won't allow that to happen, frankly."
The same day, however, a bipartisan group of US lawmakers formed the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, which will work specifically on AI regulation and safety considerations.

A significant driver of this kind of scrutiny is Anthropic itself. Company executives, including co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei, have been outspoken in their purported fears that future AI tools will become so capable they will outsmart humans, to the point where extinction is possible.
Anthropic has always put itself forward in public as an AI company that takes the safety of its technology very seriously.
Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president and sister of Dario Amodei, boasted on Thursday that the company "had an AI safety team before we launched our first product".
"AI carries real risks," she added.
Despite the company's claims that the technology it is building at a rapid pace could be dangerous, Anthropic has made one of the quickest trips from start-up to IPO in history.

articles.title: California targets Nvidia in China AI chip probe
articles.standfirst: The probe by California, where the AI chipmaker has its global headquarters, follows former CEO Jensen Huang's departure.
paragraphs: California has served an investigative subpoena on the AI chip designer Nvidia in the wake of a scandal that ended in the departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang.

The state's top law enforcement officer, attorney general Rob Bonta, said he is probing whether Nvidia or Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information, adding that such actions could violate California law if the company is found to have mislead investors and the public.
The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment.
"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said on Thursday.
This video can not be played
How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security?
Nvidia has its global headquarters in Santa Clara, California.
Earlier this month, it emerged that Huang had an extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who was an executive at the Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.
Some members of the US Congress have urged the Department of Commerce to investigate whether Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer, diverted Nvidia chips to China.
Megaspeed has previously said it is aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".
Nvidia shares have plummeted 22% since the New York Times reported on the affair in early November.

Earlier this week, the company's board chair Harvey Jones said Nvidia had no intention of reinstating  Jensen Huang after the longtime Nvidia boss and co-founder issued a statement saying he would be "honoured" to return, as some tech leaders including Elon Musk campaigned on his behalf.
Huang has acknowledged engaging in extramarital affairs – and left the company last week after reports that he had relationships with subordinates.

articles.title: Gilts v kilts: What is happening with Scottish government bonds?
articles.standfirst: MSPs have heard both the pros and cons of the government's plan to launch its first ever bond to the market.
paragraphs: The Scottish government is facing questions about its plan to issue its first ever bonds.
The move would allow ministers to borrow money from investors who in return receive regular interest payments.
The aim is to raise about £1.5bn by the end of the parliamentary term, with the funds to be used on long-term projects such as building hospitals or maintaining roads.
Named "kilts", a nod to UK government "gilts", the scheme has provoked much debate.
This week, MSPs on Holyrood's finance committee heard about the potential risks and rewards.
A bond is a financial tool used by a government to borrow money. They are sold with a promise for the buyer, or investor, to be paid back at the end of an agreed term.
The government will also make regular payments to the investor.
In the UK, a government bond is called a gilt. They are typically bought by financial institutions such as pension funds, insurance companies and commercial banks.
As a play on this term, the Scottish bonds have been nicknamed "kilts".
The Scottish government has said it expects the bonds to be issued within this financial year, subject to market conditions.

Former First Minister Humza Yousaf commissioned initial work in 2023 after advisers in the Scottish government's investor panel recommended making bonds available to the market as a means of raising Scotland's profile and attracting investment.
In November last year, the government announced that it had received an identical credit rating to the UK's score.
This was based on "prudent fiscal management" and the country's economic stability - though ministers were warned this could change if Scotland moved towards independence.
With market volatility due to conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, some have questioned whether now is a good time to launch bonds.
But at Holyrood, David McMillan, professor in finance and accounting at the University of Stirling, told MSPs: "You can't wait for a perfect time because there's going to be no perfect time."
The government wants to raise £1.5bn through bonds by 2031, although that would only be a fraction of its near £70bn budget.
About four-fifths of the Scottish government's budget is used on resource spending, which goes towards day-to-day costs such as funding the NHS, benefits payments and paying salaries.
A smaller portion is made up of capital spending, typically used on long-term physical assets such as buildings and bridges, or maintaining roads or paths.
The Scottish government is unable to borrow for resource spending other than to correct forecasting errors.
However, for capital spending, it can borrow as much as £450m a year at 2023-24 levels up to a total cap of £3bn - to be uprated with inflation.
Adjusted for inflation, the government could borrow about £491m in the current financial year, with a total limit of about £3.3bn.
Economists have noted that Scottish bonds would be a more costly way of borrowing than existing routes provided by the UK government through the National Loans Fund.
It has been estimated that interest rates on "kilts" would be 0.3 percentage points above gilts, plus an additional £2m per bond in administrative costs.

The Scottish government has not released costings, citing market sensitivities, but has insisted issuing bonds would represent value for money relative to the costs of borrowing through the UK scheme.
Ministers argue that issuing bonds would be a good opportunity to market the country to investors, and would be helpful if Scotland became independent.

Dr Ben Cormier, a senior lecturer at the University of Strathclyde's department of government and public policy, told Holyrood's finance committee that while the Scottish bonds could cost marginally more than the UK scheme, they would "bring flexibility to public finances and debt management".
McMillan agreed with the plans "in principle", but warned they would lose "credibility" with investors if limited to five years.
Cormier warned that independence was the one thing "that could materially change the nature of risk associated with Scottish bonds".
Conservative MSP Liam Kerr said bonds could be more expensive than borrowing through the National Loans Fund and voiced concerns about a lack of transparency in the programme.
McMillan agreed there should be "full information" available, saying: "You've got to have a clear, full and frank conversation with the public."

articles.title: More support for households reliant on heating oil
articles.standfirst: North Northamptonshire Council is encouraging eligible residents to apply for more support.
paragraphs: Heating oil prices have been volatile since the conflict between the US and Iran began in March
Households using heating oil as their main energy source are being offered more financial support by North Northamptonshire Council.
Residents can apply for a £250 voucher in emergency situations where low oil levels would put health, safety or basic living conditions at risk.
Heating oil is not protected by the Ofgem energy price cap, which means those reliant on it feel price increases faster than those on mains gas or electricity.
The Reform UK-led council encouraged residents to see if they were eligible for support online.
Heating oil prices have been volatile since the conflict between the US and Iran began in March.
The government announced a £53m support package in response to rising costs.
Rural areas, including parts of North Northamptonshire, are among the most affected, the council said.
Greg Wilcox, its executive member for communities and rural affairs, added: "We know that times are hard for many households and we want to do all we can to support as many residents as possible."

articles.title: How can tax and finance leaders prepare their function for an AI-enabled future?
articles.standfirst: Transforming tax and finance requires more than applying AI to existing processes. Functions have to adapt to rising regulatory demands while providing greater strategic value.
paragraphs: Transforming tax and finance requires more than applying AI to existing processes. Functions have to adapt to rising regulatory demands while providing greater strategic value. We surveyed 1,600 tax and finance executives globally, spanning 22 industries, to dig deeper into these themes, examining how leaders can combine technology, trusted data, and human judgement to build more responsive operating models.

Amidst geopolitical instability, shifting trade policies, and the expansion of digital tax administration, tax and finance teams are under growing pressure. Leaders must manage increasingly complex compliance requirements while responding quickly to changes across the markets in which their organisations operate.

At the same time, businesses expect tax and finance functions to look beyond their traditional responsibilities. Teams are being asked to identify emerging risks and contribute more directly to strategic decision-making. Our findings suggest that AI can help create the capacity needed to meet these expectations, but technology alone will not deliver transformation.

Max is based in the London office and supports the Thought Leadership team across business sectors and disciplines. Max graduated from the University of Warwick with a BA in Politics, International Studies and Quantitative Methods and an MSc in Behavioural and Data Science.

John oversees Thought Leadership projects with EMEA-based clients. He works across business sectors and disciplines, but specialises in issues relating to strategy and business operations, such as sustainability, digital transformation, employment and skills, finance, and performance management. He has directed the Thought Leadership contribution on some of Oxford Economics’ largest and most complex research programmes, for global consultancies and corporates, including Accenture, the Adecco Group, Cognizant, EY, Fujitsu and YouTube. Often this is in collaboration with his economist colleagues to blend qualitative and quantitative analysis, and to explore the impact of corporate actions at a business, industry and economy level.

John joined Oxford Economics in 2014, after 25 years as a Financial Controller, financial management consultant and, most recently, a thought leadership expert for IBM’s Institute for Business Value, focused on global public sector issues. John then worked on the independent Digital Government Review as input to the UK General Election. He is an Economics graduate from Sussex University and a Chartered Management Accountant (ACMA).

Alice Ramoff is a Research Intern within the Thought Leadership team based in London. Her current role focuses on business research and AI. Prior to joining Oxford Economics, Alice worked for a technology start-up focused on food sustainability. She holds a Master's degree from the University of Edinburgh and a Bachelor's degree from King's College London.

articles.title: Spain’s 2026 Election: Diverging Tax Agendas and the Push for Full Expensing
articles.standfirst: Spain’s 2026 election presents a clear divide in economic policy, with the Socialist Workers' Party favoring higher taxes on capital and businesses, while the People’s Party and Vox advocate tax cuts to encourage investment, stimulate economic growth, and improve competitiveness.
paragraphs: As Spain approaches the November 2026 general election, voters face a choice between competing visions for the country’s economic future. While housing, immigration, and infrastructure security are expected to dominate campaign headlines, taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. policy may prove to be one of the election’s most consequential economic dividing lines.

The debate comes after a period of significant tax policy change under Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez. Since 2018, Spain has introduced a digital services tax (DST), a financial transaction tax, a solidarity wealth taxA wealth tax is imposed on an individual’s net wealth, or the market value of their total owned assets minus liabilities. A wealth tax can be narrowly or widely defined, and depending on the definition of wealth, the base for a wealth tax can vary., a domestic minimum tax, and several sector-specific levies. Over the same period, Spain’s standing in international tax competitiveness deteriorated markedly, falling from 27th place in 2017 to 35th out of 38 Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries in the 2026 International Tax Competitiveness Index (ITCI), fueling debate over whether the current tax framework supports long-term economic growth and investment.

The main parties offer sharply different answers. The governing Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) has generally favored higher taxes on capital, wealth, financial institutions, and large businesses, while the center-right Partido Popular (PP) and Vox advocate lower taxes on investment, income, and wealth, arguing that stronger growth is the best path to higher living standards and sustainable public finances. The election presents voters a choice between maintaining the current approach or shifting toward a more investment-oriented tax system.

Although smaller parties could influence the final outcome, PSOE, PP, and Vox currently lead the polls and represent the clearest alternatives on tax policy. This analysis focuses on their competing proposals and what they would mean for Spain’s tax system and economic competitiveness.

The PP’s economic program proposes a broad package of tax relief measures for households, entrepreneurs, investors, and businesses. Its plans include lower personal income taxes through higher personal and family allowances, targeted tax cuts for middle- and lower-income households, and refundable family tax credits. The party also supports automatic inflationInflation is when the general price of goods and services increases across the economy, reducing the purchasing power of a currency and the value of certain assets. The same paycheck covers less goods, services, and bills. It is sometimes referred to as a “hidden tax,” as it leaves taxpayers less well-off due to higher costs and “bracket creep,” while increasing the government’s spendin indexation for minimum-wage earners and periodic indexation of income tax bracketsA tax bracket is the range of incomes taxed at given rates, which typically differ depending on filing status. In a progressive individual or corporate income tax system, rates rise as income increases. There are seven federal individual income tax brackets; the federal corporate income tax system is flat. to prevent fiscal drag. In addition, it proposes income tax rebates for young workers.

It also advocates a temporary 0 percent value-added tax (VAT) rate on basic food, VAT exemptions for small businesses with turnover below €85,000, and stronger tax incentives for research, innovation, and productivity-enhancing investment. In addition, it would remove investment-disincentivizing taxes, strengthen anti-tax-evasion measures with revenues recycled into further tax cuts, ensure neutral taxation of savings vehicles, and protect the tax autonomy of Spain’s Autonomous Communities. This stance could also imply the elimination of the solidarity wealth tax, which the party has consistently opposed.

The party’s housing agenda seeks to reduce the cost of housing for young people. Their proposal includes cutting VAT on first-home young buyers, seeking agreements with regional governments to reduce property transfer taxes on existing homes, and introducing a tax-favored “Young Home Savings Account,” allowing annual contributions of up to €2,000 with a 20 percent tax deductionA tax deduction allows taxpayers to subtract certain deductible expenses and other items to reduce how much of their income is taxed, which reduces how much tax they owe. For individuals, some deductions are available to all taxpayers, while others are reserved only for taxpayers who itemize. For businesses, most business expenses are fully and immediately deductible in the year they occur, but ot and tax-free returns when used to purchase a first home. For renters, the party would introduce an income tax deduction for tenants, with larger benefits for lower-income households. Landlords who renew leases for at least three additional years and limit rent increases below inflation would receive an income tax deduction or tax creditA tax credit is a provision that reduces a taxpayer’s final tax bill, dollar-for-dollar. A tax credit differs from deductions and exemptions, which reduce taxable income rather than the taxpayer’s tax bill directly..

However, perhaps the most economically significant proposal is Measure 181: expanding immediate expensing for business investment. The PP proposes allowing companies to fully deduct in the year incurred investments in machinery, equipment, digitalization, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, software, and patents. It would also allow innovative firms without current profits to access part of the incentive upfront.

This proposal represents a substantial shift toward investment neutrality and faster cost recoveryCost recovery refers to how the tax system permits businesses to recover the cost of investments through depreciation or amortization. Depreciation and amortization deductions affect taxable income, effective tax rates, and investment decisions..

Under normal corporate tax systems, companies often recover investment costs over many years through depreciationDepreciation is a measurement of the “useful life” of a business asset, such as machinery or a factory, to determine the multiyear period over which the cost of that asset can be deducted from taxable income. Instead of allowing businesses to deduct the cost of investments immediately (i.e., full expensing), depreciation requires deductions to be taken over time, reducing their value and disco schedules. Inflation and the time value of money reduce the real value of those deductions, effectively increasing the tax burden on new investment.

Full expensing eliminates this distortion by allowing firms to deduct the entire cost of qualifying investments immediately. Full expensing is one of the most growth-friendly business tax reforms because it lowers the tax penalty on investment while maintaining taxation of profits.
Our modeling suggest that full expensing for machinery and equipment and intellectual property would meaningfully improve Spain’s investment climate.

The reform significantly reduces the tax burden on new investment. The asset-wide marginal effective tax rate falls from 14.2 percent to 11.6 percent. By lowering the cost of capital by 1.6 percentage points, the reform is projected to increase business investment by 1.9 percent and expand the non-financial corporate capital stock by 2.8 percent. These gains would boost productivity, raising long-run GDP by 1.1 percent, wages by 0.93 percent, and the aggregate wage bill by 1.1 percent, while employment would increase only modestly (0.14 percent). The results suggest that the reform’s main benefits would come through higher capital investment, productivity, and wages rather than stronger employment growth, an important distinction for an economy that has faced weak productivity growth over the past two decades.

Additionally, the fiscal cost of accelerated depreciation is front-loaded, peaking in the early years and declining rapidly thereafter, since it only brings capital allowances forward without increasing their total nominal value. As a result, full expensing is one of the most cost-effective tax reforms, delivering significant investment incentives for a relatively low long-term fiscal cost.

While the full expensing proposal would have a significant impact on the Spanish economy and improve the neutrality of the Spanish tax system, other PP’s reform proposals move in the opposite direction. A temporary 0 percent VAT on basic foods (meat, fish, and conserves) would narrow the VAT base by 4.9 percentage points from 44.9 to 40 percent of potential taxable consumption and would cost around €4.4 billion annually, in 2025 prices. Additionally, the VAT exemptions for small businesses would further reduce the VAT base. This means that small businesses below the threshold are not required to collect VAT on their outputs sold to customers but will then also not receive a refund for VAT paid on business inputs. However, small businesses with negative VAT liability will tend to register voluntarily even when below the threshold.
If the PP’s tax agenda seeks to improve investment incentives, Vox offers a much more aggressive tax-cutting platform.

Vox’s fiscal agenda is centered on broad-based tax cuts, deregulation, and stronger incentives for work, investment, and family formation. The party proposes lower personal income taxes and VAT rates, a reduction in the corporate tax rate, lighter taxation of energy consumption, and a systematic review of all taxes and fees affecting households and businesses. It also advocates a zero Social-Security contribution for self-employed workers earning below the minimum wage and lower contributions above that threshold.

While Vox’s current manifesto provides few quantitative details, earlier proposals offer a clearer picture of its fiscal agenda. In previous plans, Vox advocated reducing the standard VAT rate from 21 percent to 18 percent. Its proposed corporate tax rate of 15 percent would place Spain among the lowest-rate corporate tax jurisdictions in Europe. On personal income taxation, Vox previously proposed exempting income up to €22,000, replacing the current central government tax system with just two tax brackets: 15 percent on income up to €70,000, and 25 percent on income above that threshold. Currently, the central income tax brackets go from 9.5 percent to 24.5 percent. The plan also included an additional four-percentage-point reduction in income tax liability for each dependent child, underscoring the party’s emphasis on supporting families through the tax code.

The party’s housing agenda has some similarities with PP’s housing tax proposal. Vox would also eliminate taxes on first-home purchases through a 0 percent VAT rate on new homes and a 100 percent exemption from the property transfer tax on existing homes, while restoring the homeownership tax deduction. The party also proposes tax incentives for long-term rentals, lower taxes on housing development and construction, and preferential tax treatment for investments that increase rental supply. A key difference from the PP is that Vox would partly finance its housing tax cuts by increasing taxes on speculative property transactions and purchases by non-EU buyers.

A key challenge for Vox would be financing these tax cuts while preserving fiscal sustainability in a country already burdened by large deficits, high public debt, and growing pension costs. That said, our modeling suggests the proposed reforms could stimulate investment and economic activity, expanding the tax baseThe tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates. and partially offsetting the initial revenue losses through higher tax collections over time.

Our modeling results suggest that the proposed Vox tax package, combining a reduction in Spain’s CIT rate and standard VAT rate, would deliver a notable boost to economic activity by improving investment incentives and lowering the tax burden on work and consumption. The corporate tax cut reduces the marginal effective tax rate on new investment from 14.2 percent to 7.5 percent, lowering the cost of capital by around 5.1 percent and driving most of the overall macroeconomic gains. As a result of these two tax reforms, long-run GDP will increase by 3.7 percent, investment by 6.5 percent, and the non-financial corporate capital stock by 9.5 percent, while the wage bill rises by 3.7 percent and employment by 0.7 percent.

The VAT reduction provides an additional, though smaller, stimulus by reducing the labor tax wedgeBroadly speaking, a tax wedge is the difference between the pre-tax price or return and after-tax price or return. For labor income, it is the difference between the total labor costs to the employer and the corresponding net take-home pay of the employee. and encouraging labor supply. Specifically, the proposed reduction in the standard VAT rate is estimated to result in an annual revenue loss of approximately €6.4 billion, in 2025 euros, equivalent to around 6.8 percent of VAT receipts. Although this makes Vox’s proposal approximately €2 billion more expensive than the PP’s proposed VAT reduction on basic goods, it also improves VAT efficiency by reducing tax-induced distortions and increasing the C-efficiency ratio from 44.9 to 48.7 percent. Nevertheless, VAT revenues are estimated to fall by only 3.9 percent, rather than the full 6.8 percent, as the stronger economic activity generated by the CIT rate cut expands the consumption taxA consumption tax is typically levied on the purchase of goods or services and is paid directly or indirectly by the consumer in the form of retail sales taxes, excise taxes, tariffs, value-added taxes (VAT), or income taxes where all savings are tax-deductible. base and partially offsets the revenue loss.

Overall, the results indicate that this reform package could significantly strengthen Spain’s long-term growth prospects, with the corporate income taxA corporate income tax (CIT) is levied by federal and state governments on business profits. Many companies are not subject to the CIT because they are taxed as pass-through businesses, with income reportable under the individual income tax. reduction accounting for most of the positive economic effects.

Additionally, Vox’s proposed income tax reform, which would reduce the marginal tax wedge by 6.35 percentage points at an estimated cost of €48 billion, could significantly boost economic activity. By increasing workers’ after-tax earnings, the reform raises employment by 2.7 percent, investment by 3 percent, and long-run GDP by almost 3 percent. The resulting economic expansion would broaden the tax base and stimulate consumption, generating an estimated 3 percent increase in VAT revenues (approximately €2.85 billion) that would partially offset the fiscal cost of the proposed tax cuts.

Nevertheless, the reform raises significant concerns regarding fiscal sustainability. With an estimated cost of €48 billion, it is among the most expensive tax reform proposals. Although stronger economic growth would generate additional tax revenues, these gains are unlikely to fully offset the initial revenue loss. Without complementary spending cuts or alternative revenue measures, the reform could widen Spain’s budget deficit and increase public debt, raising questions about its long-term fiscal stability.

PSOE’s fiscal agenda largely builds on its current approach, combining higher taxes on wealth, capital, large corporations, and other perceived undertaxed sectors with targeted tax relief aimed at lower- and middle-income households. Key measures include increasing the taxation of capital income above current levels, with a top rate of 35 percent (from the current 30 percent) applying to capital income exceeding €300,000. This 5-percentage-point increase builds on a trend that began in 2019, bringing the cumulative increase to 12 percentage points if implemented. The manifesto also proposes expanding the existing DST and introducing new taxes on large technology companies and certain AI-related activities.

It plans to continue increasing business taxation and it proposes a new surcharge on listed companies where CEO compensation exceeds 100 times the median employee salary, with an additional tier for pay ratios above 200:1. The party would strengthen wealth taxation and double the financial transactions tax, increasing the Tobin tax rate from 0.2 percent to 0.4 percent. In parallel, it proposes new levies on luxury goods consumption with a significant carbon footprint, including private jets, mega yachts, and business-class flights, targeting what it describes as high-income and environmentally intensive consumption.

At the household level, PSOE program includes refundable tax credits for dependent children, continued tax protection for workers on low earnings or around the minimum wage, and temporary progressive income-tax deductions during periods of elevated inflation. Housing policy also highlights a clear divide while PP and Vox largely favor a “carrot” approach, using tax cuts, deductions, and incentives to encourage homeownership and expand rental supply; whereas PSOE leans more heavily on the “stick,” using higher taxes and penalties on vacant properties, speculative holdings, and large landlords to influence housing market behavior.

A key risk of PSOE’s approach is that higher taxes on capital, investment, and businesses could slow growth while raising less revenue than expected, as many of the new taxes target narrow tax bases. Combined with higher spending commitments, any revenue shortfall could eventually create pressure for broader tax increases or higher deficits.

The election debate raises a broader question: should Spain prioritize redistribution or competitiveness? Or more aptly put: could a more competitive tax system broaden the tax base sufficiently to generate greater revenues and, in turn, support more redistribution?
Voters face a clear choice among three competing tax policy models.
PSOE, the incumbent party, would largely continue the current approach of higher taxes on capital, wealth, financial transactions, and businesses to finance additional public spending.

The PP’s program focuses on improving investment and productivity. Rather than providing targeted subsidies or government spending programs, it seeks to improve economic performance by removing a tax barrier to investment through full expensing.
Meanwhile, Vox proposes a broader low-tax strategy centered on lower taxes on work, investment, business activity, and consumption with a higher initial revenue cost.

From an economic-growth perspective, the strongest proposals are those that improve incentives to invest, work, and save. The modeling results suggest that reforms such as full expensing, lower corporate tax rates, and lower taxes on labor income would boost investment, productivity, wages, and GDP more effectively than additional taxes on capital and business activity. By contrast, many of PSOE’s proposed tax increases target narrow tax bases that are unlikely to generate sufficient revenue, while discouraging investment, constraining economic growth, and encouraging capital flight.

Regardless of the election outcome, Spain would benefit from a broader pro-growth tax reform agenda. Policymakers should avoid further tax increases and consider introducing permanent full expensing and repealing several distortionary taxes introduced during the Sánchez administration, including the windfall profits taxA windfall profits tax is a one-time surtax levied on a company or industry when economic conditions result in large and unexpected profits. Historically, such taxes have targeted oil and energy companies when costs have risen, especially from war or other crises., DST, financial transactions tax, domestic minimum tax, solidarity wealth tax, and wealth taxes.

Our modeling estimates that eliminating Spain’s DST could boost GDP by 0.036 percent (€539 million annually), while increasing investment, wages, and employment. Notably, the estimated economic gains would be 67 percent greater than the tax’s current annual revenue of €323 million. The resulting expansion would broaden the tax base and generate additional revenues from other taxes, partially offsetting the initial revenue loss.

Combined with reducing the top tax rate on capital gains and dividends from 30 percent to 23 percent, these reforms would improve Spain’s investment environment and move the country from 35th to 20th place in the International Tax Competitiveness Index, making the tax system more supportive of long-term growth, investment, and rising wages. More broadly, the 2026 election will present voters with a consequential choice between competing visions for Spain’s tax system, with implications for the country’s long-term growth, investment, tax competitiveness, and wage growth.
Subscribe to our free newsletter to get the latest tax data, news and analysis.

Cristina Enache writes on the economics of tax policy and is the author of the Spanish Regional Tax Competitiveness Index. She was formerly the Director of Research at Civismo, an economic research organization based in Spain. She also served as head of research at Institución Futuro, a regional think tank based in Navarra in northern Spain. She is also currently Secretary-General at the World Taxpayers Associations and General Manager of the Spanish Taxpayers Union, which she joined in 2016.

articles.title: Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?
articles.standfirst: Anthropic's hotly anticipated IPO is expected to put it in the top 10 most valuable US companies, but the future is uncertain.
paragraphs: Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?
It was during November 2020 that somewhere in San Francisco, a woman called Daniela Amodei phoned a friend, asking for advice.
Daniela oversaw safety and policy at OpenAI, one of the most talked-about AI companies in the world.
But Daniela and her brother Dario - who worked there too - had misgivings over safety levels at OpenAI and thought it could be time to walk away.

So she did what many do when we can't make a decision about something, she phoned a friend. The friend's reply was direct and to the point: "You don't need to be on the phone with me. You already know the answer."
The Amodei siblings and a handful of other colleagues quit. Together, they set up a rival – Anthropic.
Six years on and Anthropic, the maker of leading AI model Claude, has predicted revenues of $52bn in 2026 and $135bn in 2027, according to analyst estimates.

It is selling shares to the public for the first time in what's known as an Initial Public Offering or IPO, aiming for a valuation of an estimated $1.4tn (£1tn), which would propel it straight into the top 10 of the most valuable US companies.
The sale comes at a crucial time when many are wondering whether, amid increasing concern about the potential of AI, the industry's bubble is showing signs of bursting.

Where once investors were "all in" on a technological revolution to rival the railroads, the car, electricity and the internet, some are now hedging their bets, amid arguments that AI prices will be driven down as the technology becomes more common and concerns that a hefty wedge of the AI investment is tech giants investing in each other.

Shares in companies that supply the raw computing power behind AI, like Coreweave and Nebius, have seen their value cut in half while even the mighty Nvidia has lost its crown as the world's most valuable company with its shares down 30% - a staggering $2tn fall in value.
So could the Anthropic IPO reinflate the bubble or will it be remembered as the last gasp of a boom that is heading for a bust?
At an event last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told JPMorgan Chase's CEO Jamie Dimon that his guiding principle was to "never let your company be worth a single dollar more than it's worth".

The company is selling roughly $81bn worth of shares to the general public and a further $26bn on to other big tech companies. It is comfortably the single biggest money raising event in US corporate history.
Good Bad Billionaire
9 November 2026

It's an old adage that during a gold rush you should buy companies that sell the picks and shovels as opposed to those staking everything on striking gold. In AI's case that's the chip makers, the data centre builders, the energy providers. But Anthropic is arguably the gold itself and this IPO will see what value people put on it, according to Fiona Cincotta from StoneX trading.

"I think the reason that this IPO is so important is basically it's the first ability for the public investors to access a pure play AI trade," she says, adding that previous offerings have been about "other parts of the ecosystem, which are, the semiconductors, the chips, the, data centres. But this is the first time that we were actually able to access the AI provider."
Daniela Amodei helped set up a rival company to OpenAI
What a company is worth depends almost entirely on predicted future earnings.
It's that calculation that many think presents the sharpest needle to the AI bubble.

Will current and future users of AI be prepared to pay enough to justify the trillions being spent on the chips, data centres, energy and employees, some of whom can command annual salaries of over $100m?

"AI is certainly in a financial bubble. While LLMs [large language models] offer genuine utility and are undoubtedly here to stay, the economics don't add up," said Gary Marcus, Professor Emeritus at New York University and author of Taming Silicon Valley, speaking earlier this year.
"[The] more companies build AI models, the [more the] technology becomes commoditised, eliminating meaningful competitive advantages and driving down prices."
So far, the growth rates in Anthropic revenue are extraordinary.
But these explosive growth rates hide a potential problem. Around a quarter of that revenue came from just a handful of companies, among them Google and Amazon.
It's also concentrated in the US which accounts for two-thirds of its revenue.

There is also the staggering network of circular financing found in the AI world. For example, Anthropic has agreements to buy or lease hundreds of billions of dollars worth of chips and computing power from a handful of companies including Broadcom, Google, Amazon. Many of those firms are also investors in Anthropic and major customers of its products.
It's not just some Wall Street investors questioning whether the AI boom is all it's cracked up to be. Out on Main Street, ordinary Americans have concerns too.

With the US driving so much of global AI growth, a growing public backlash against a technology that threatens to replace millions of jobs and hoover up vast amounts of energy and water became a factor in the recent midterm elections in the US.

Many areas in the US have passed moratoriums on data centre development and many candidates deemed too close to big tech found that association a political liability rather than an asset. Many Democrat candidates publicly opposed data centre development and won.

Added to that, the Pied Piper of AI, chip maker Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang, resigned last week after admitting to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang and another with a company executive who reported to him.
Dario Amodei is one of Silicon Valley's big beasts

Huang's spectacular fall from grace and Nvidia's 30% fall in value from its peak have left AI investors looking for a new champion for the AI boom that has underpinned the US stock market and arguably much of its entire economy for the last two years.
If Anthropic and its CEO are to be AI's new Pied Piper, he will be playing a different tune to the relentlessly upbeat, leather jacket-clad talisman Huang.

While Huang wanted AI development to continue full throttle, Anthropic was built on misgivings over the levels of safety and responsibility the OpenAI leavers felt were being exercised over the development of society-changing technology.
Amodei has warned that AI capabilities could enable biological weapon development, mass surveillance, authoritarianism and the replacement of millions of white-collar, tax-paying workers.
He has called for a slowdown in its development as its powers are growing at such an exponential rate that it could very soon elude any human oversight.

That said, his paternalistic overtures have been sceptically received by those who point out that the pace of Anthropic's development of new more powerful models has shown no sign of the slowdown he's advocating for the rest of the industry.

But for all the concerns, just as with Elon Musk's SpaceX before it, the hype and the FOMO (fear of missing out) on an undoubtedly profound moment in technological and perhaps human development, means that buying interest is high.
It's reported that orders to buy shares exceed the number on offer by over six times.
With demand outstripping supply by such a margin, a first-day jump is to be expected given the oversubscription, but it doesn't tell you much about long-run return.
Using SpaceX as an example again, shares initially rose nearly 70% from its IPO sale price of $135 to $225. Shares in SpaceX are currently back to $145.
The Anthropic IPO could be wildly successful and blow a bit of fresh new air into what some maintain still looks a lot like a bubble.
Eileen Burbidge, founder of tech investors Passion Capital, is one of those who reject the notion that AI is a bubble about to burst.

"Maybe the growth of the bubble has slowed down a little bit, but actually I wouldn't be willing to say that it's about to burst yet," says Burbidge. "I think this IPO could actually mean everyone could be off to the races again."

Fiona Cincotta believes Anthropic's IPO is about far more than just Anthropic. "I think what's going to be really interesting here is I think it can actually be used as a valuation benchmark for the entire AI ecosystem," she says.
"That's why I don't think this is just going to affect the share price of Anthropic. I think this is going to have much wider implications across the whole AI trade."

Two things can be true at the same time. The Anthropic IPO could be wildly successful - FOMO is a powerful emotion in financial markets. But its probable success won't soothe the unease in some quarters that not every company, every investor and every citizen will think of AI as the answer to humanity's problems.

articles.title: The seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multi-billionaires
articles.standfirst: The AI company behind Claude is about to sell its shares on the US stock market - making its founders very rich.
paragraphs: Brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei are chief executive and president of Anthropic
In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.
The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.
Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at $83 each, it said on Wednesday.
At that price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $19.3bn (£14.7bn) each.
So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?
In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT.
He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.

Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track, and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.
Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.
Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.
But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.
Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".
Listen: Dario Amodei BBC Sounds profile
Dario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.
She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian.
Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright.
She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations.
The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work.
Tom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture.
He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project.
Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends.
He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity".
Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources.
Jack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America.

Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.
He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director.
Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.
Jared Kaplan, 42, is chief science officer at Anthropic, and heads its technical research. He is also an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore.
He holds a PhD in physics from Harvard University.

His work on scaling laws - which describe mathematical patterns that show that bigger AI models trained on more data tend to be more consistent - has helped provide AI firms with a framework for predicting AI behaviour, according to Anthropic.
Chris Olah is described as "interpretability research lead" primarily focused on how AI models work with each other.
But according to the New York Times, Olah has spent much of the last year convening meetings with faith leaders from across the religious spectrum.
Described by the newspaper as "boyish" but with "the zeal of an evangelist" the 34-year-old is reportedly exploring the relationship between morality and AI.
He previously led interoperability research at OpenAI, and prior to that was a research scientist at Google Brain.
The Canadian left the University of Toronto early, but later secured a Thiel Fellowship of $100,000, which is a scholarship to help gifted people move into research without a degree.

Sam McCandlish, 36, takes less of a public-facing role than the other founders, but like them will own around 1.6% of the company after its shares go on sale. As a result he too will see his stake crystallise into a hugely valuable asset.
McCandlish is Anthropic's chief architect, and helps shape and implement the company's policy designed to mitigate the risks of AI. Prior to this he worked on safety at OpenAI.
He has a physics PhD from Stanford, and maths and physics degree from Brandeis University outside Boston.
