articles.title: Typical energy bill forecast to go up by £443 a year from January as inflation rate rises again
articles.standfirst: Energy bills are expected to jump by 26% a year for a typical household as UK inflation hits its highest rate for a year.
paragraphs: Gas and electricity bills for a typical household are forecast to jump by £443 a year from January as the inflation rate rose to its highest level in a year.
A typical annual bill is predicted to rise by 26% in the new year, according to consultancy Cornwall Insight, ahead of the official announcement next week.
Some households will get a £100 payment to help with the rising cost of living, a policy which was announced in the Budget.
Prices rose 3.6% in the year to October, up from 3.5% in September mainly because of higher petrol and diesel prices, official figures show.
Inflation has been driven higher in recent months as the US-Israel war with Iran has driven up the cost of energy and fuel.
In response to prices surging, the Bank of England raised interest rates for the first time in three years earlier this month, in a bid to slow inflation to its target of 2%.
Interest rates increased from 3.75% to 4%, and the Bank signalled a further rise could be likely unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved.
Higher interest rates lift the cost of borrowing for some mortgages, loans and credit cards, but can also lead to a better return on savings.
Emma Reynolds, chief secretary to the Treasury, said the government was providing help for households with energy costs.
VAT has been cut on electricity bills to zero until next July and the government will also hand £100 to 20 million homes in January.

But with annual household energy bills forecast to reach £2,166, Cornwall Insight's retail markets principal, Craig Lowrey, said that "ultimately this support can only chip away at the edges of a bill that continues to be pushed up by events in the Middle East".
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, said: "Affordability is my number one priority, and I will continue driving towards cheap, clean power."
Sophie, who manages a cafe in Brighton, told the BBC she watches her smart meter at home "like a hawk".
"I'm very conscious of the cost of energy, and it is having an impact on how we function in the home as a family," she said.
"I try to cook using the oven a lot less than I used to. We haven't got the heating on yet in our household. We're just like 'wear more layers'. We've got electric blankets on the sofa."
Shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, said four successive rises in the inflation rate was down to the UK's "soaring energy costs" and Labour's decision to "hike taxes and employment costs".
Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the ONS, said fuel prices were "once again a major contributor" to the increase in the inflation rate in October.
Rising energy prices can lead to more expensive food and staples for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs.
Earlier this month, the Bank of England said there had been "limited evidence" of this, with some firms absorbing cost increases and accepting lower profit margins.
But Fitzner said on Wednesday: "Annual costs of both raw materials and goods leaving factories continue to climb, driven by higher crude oil and petrol prices, respectively."
Petrol prices rose by 5.2p per litre between September and October, the ONS said, with the average price last month hitting 174.7p per litre - the highest since August 2022.
Diesel prices, meanwhile, reached the highest price since records began 30 years ago, averaging 199.5p per litre in October.
But the ONS said price inflation in restaurants and cafes had slowed last month, and that prices had fallen on average for hotels.
And food price inflation rose by 0.9%, the slowest pace in five years.
Core inflation, which strips out energy and food costs, and services inflation were little changed on last month. The figure is closely watched by the Bank of England when setting interest rates.
It could mean the Bank opts to hold off on a further rate rise in December, though policymakers believe inflation could peak at 4.9% in the middle of next year and not return to 2% until 2028.
In an "adverse scenario", where the US-Iran war could escalate further and send oil prices higher, inflation could reach 6.2% in 2027, it has suggested.

A spokesperson for the Bank said it decided to raise rates two weeks ago to "limit how much higher energy costs affect other prices, and will continue to set interest rates to make sure inflation returns to the 2% target and stays there".
Additional reporting by Raphael Sheridan, economics producer
How is the rising cost of living affecting your quality of life?

articles.title: Heating bills, chocolate and cat food: What the inflation figures mean for you
articles.standfirst: Prices are rising at their fastest pace for a year in the UK, and higher energy costs are on the way.
paragraphs: Nobody will be celebrating the fact that prices in the UK are rising at the fastest pace for a year.
Add to that an expectation of higher household energy bills and sharpening price increases and things look grim for everyone.
But there are some signs of hope that may take the edge off the rising cost of living. Here's how.
That headline is not missing a decimal point. The latest prediction for the increase in domestic energy prices in the new year is, indeed, 26%.

Millions of homes in England, Scotland and Wales are on tariffs affected by regulator Ofgem's price cap, which is set every three months. The next change for January will be officially announced next Wednesday, 25 November.

Energy consultancy Cornwall Insight, which has a good track record with its predictions, suggests that a household using a typical amount of gas and electricity will pay £2,166 a year - that's an increase of £443 from current levels.
Not all energy use for the year is between January and March, but a big chunk is owing to the cold, dark days and nights.
How much you pay depends on your use, with heavy users of gas likely to be the hardest hit.
The government has promised a £100 payment for people living in homes in council tax bands A to D in England to help cover winter energy costs. Other nations are planning similar support.
The latest inflation data shows that government assistance can have an impact on the general rate of inflation, as recorded by the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
Domestic energy prices rose by nearly 4% in October, but this was offset in inflationary terms by a cut in VAT on electricity bills.
While the rate of inflation in general was 3.6% in the year to October, food prices only went up by 0.9%.
So why the difference?
It is partly the result of intense competition between the supermarkets. Like many retailers, they are facing higher costs but are not passing that onto their customers in full.
There may be some scars from the recent cost-of-living spike here. Shoppers suffered a period during the big rise in inflation in 2022-23 when food prices rocketed.
Those higher prices are embedded. While food prices overall aren't coming down now, they aren't rising anywhere near as fast as back then.
The detail here is very interesting. Take chocolate: world cocoa prices are down since 2024, and now chocolate prices are falling - down 2.9%, according to the latest data.
But the ONS has also pointed to cat food as one, albeit small, driver of the faster rate of rising prices.

Should high energy and fuel costs - which are driving the rising rate of inflation - persist, there are questions over whether the cost of producing and transporting food also goes up, and the chances of that higher cost being passed on to consumers are greater.

Economists have been closely studying whether there are any signs of those so-called second-round effects - where an initial price shock spreads to wages, services and broader consumer prices. So far, there are relatively few.
Food is, of course, a necessity.

If prices rise then it takes a bigger chunk of people's income and so has a deeper impact on those whose finances are already stretched, so the latest data on food prices is good news for many people.

One set of economists who will consider whether there is evidence of second-round effects are the nine people who set interest rates, which heavily influences the cost of borrowing money - such as mortgages - as well as the returns people get on savings.
The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee meets again in December and, after that, in February.
Having just raised interest rates - for the first time in more than three years - to 4%, there's a widespread expectation among analysts that another hike is to come.
To be clear, we don't know if and when that will happen for sure.
The case for an increase would be if prices continue to accelerate. The Bank will want to slow that down.
The case against would be price rises remaining relatively confined to energy-related costs. Any easing of Middle East tensions could limit price rises without Bank of England intervention.
As far as wages are concerned, the latest official data suggests that rising prices are largely covered by rising pay.
That is an average - so is not true for everyone - but how long it remains the case may be key to how deep upcoming price rises cut into our personal finances.
How is the rising cost of living affecting your quality of life?

articles.title: Nvidia says it won't reinstate Huang as it reports soaring sales
articles.standfirst: The AI chip giant reported strong quarterly earnings on Tuesday after the dramatic exit of Jensen Huang.
paragraphs: Jensen Huang and Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress
Nvidia has firmly ruled out letting ousted co-founder Jensen Huang return as it revealed that sales doubled to more than $100bn.

In the company's first results since Huang's dramatic exit last week, covering the three month period just before the recent scandal surfaced, interim chief executive Colette Kress said it was "business as usual". She told investors: "We've got this."
Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said he would be "honoured" to return and lead Nvidia, having quit following alleged extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected spy for China.
But Nvidia's chair Harvey Jones said: "The board does not intend to reinstate him."
Nvidia reported that sales for the three months to 25 October rose to $115.8bn (£86.9bn), with shares in the company jumping by 4.8% in after-hours trading.
The company's profits also doubled from a year ago rising to $65bn. Sales from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn.
The company said its rapid growth is poised to continue and revenue will rise by another 13% in the next quarter.
Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure that Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worries that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader.

"The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment."
This video can not be played
Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?
Kress seemed eager to stress that Nvidia can continue to not only succeed, but lead the ongoing AI buildout that is happening throughout the technology industry.
"It is business as usual," she said. "Our partners, our suppliers, all of them are 100% behind us."
She added that Nvidia's leadership team has "stood up very strongly over the last week... working seamlessly in all of their departments and projects".

"Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed." Kress said before leaving the analyst call. "We've got this."
The interim chief executive also said Nvidia is no longer shipping Hopper data centre semiconductors to China.
The Hopper technology is in Nvidia's advanced H200 processors, which the firm won approval to sell in China after Huang's repeated lobbying efforts in Washington.
They had previously been restricted over concerns that selling them to China would give its industries and military an edge over the US.
Kress did not elaborate on why the shipments had been stopped.
Jones saying earlier that the company would not answer analysts' questions about Huang or Nvidia's investigation into his conduct, he did address the search for a permanent replacement.
He said Nvidia is working with an executive search firm and is considering internal and external candidates, but that the company would not rush its selection.

"With the advanced technology and the national security dynamics in the marketplace, our new chief executive will have to navigate those waters carefully," Jones said. "The search will be thorough and we want to do it as quickly as possible, but we won't do it before we find the exact right person."
Michael Monaghan from investment firm Founder ETFs is among those who want Huang back in the top job at Nvidia.
The Nvidia investor told the BBC that he is waiting to see the results of a thorough investigation into Huang's actions, instead of relying on "salacious allegations" made in the media.
Nvidia's strong earnings are "from the machine that Jensen built" and a company tends to lose "its shine and vision" after an iconic founder leaves, Monaghan said.

articles.title: How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy?
articles.standfirst: The former Nvidia chief executive has been at the centre of the artificial intelligence boom.
paragraphs: Nvidia and its co-founder Jensen Huang have been at the centre of the artificial intelligence (AI) spending boom.

No company or chief executive has arguably been more consequential to the development of AI in recent years, with the US microchip manufacturer under Huang positioning itself as a critical cog in the development of the world-changing technology.
That partnership has now ended following Huang's resignation over revelations of extramarital affairs, one of which is alleged to have been with a Chinese spy.
The company has been rocked by the scandal, with hundreds of billions of dollars wiped off its stock market value and questions swirling about the extent of the impact of Huang's departure.
While Nvidia is not as much of a household name as other Big Tech players such as Apple, Amazon and Microsoft, the company has been just as integral to the booming US stock market of recent years.
The billions of dollars being funnelled into AI and the construction of data centres has bolstered the American economy, with Nvidia being one of the biggest spenders.
Originally focusing on chips which process graphics for computer games, it pivoted to making the chips used in AI systems and now dominates the market.
It is now one the most valuable firms, worth $3.8 trillion (£2.9 trillion), and on Tuesday said its rapid growth is poised to continue as the firm's quarterly sales doubled from a year earlier.

But there's now an air of uncertainty over Nvidia's future direction. Huang played a major role in the company, leading its shift towards AI, and maintained a firm grip on the company, with up to 200 people directly reporting to him.

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at investment firm AJ Bell, says because Huang was also a key figure in "flying the flag" to drum up enthusiasm and investment for the wider AI industry, his departure posed a "real risk" that Nvidia could now decide to change its current strategy and rein in spending.
Such a move could spell a wider slowdown in AI investment, which would have an economic impact. How big? That's "unknown", Coatsworth says.

"If they decide to go with the much more cautious route... there could be a knock-on effect in that you have got various companies in the AI infrastructure space suddenly finding they don't have a key source of finance," he says.

Kunjan Sobhani, senior technology industry analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, expects the impact of Huang leaving to be "limited" for now as Nvidia has strong commitments and a deep order book. But he said this picture could change in the long run.
That is because Nvidia, on its journey to the top of the AI industry, has created a spider's web of deals through what is known as "circular financing".

Not only does it sell microchips to its customers, which include the likes of Meta, SpaceX and OpenAI, it has also provided funds for them and other firms in the supply chain by either handing out loans or investing in them directly.

The practice has prompted concerns among some investors, who worry what might happen if Nvidia were to turn off the spending taps. If investment dried up, would other firms in the supply chain cut spending or jobs themselves? Would that spread to the wider US economy?
That risk is perhaps why tech bosses including Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, the CEO of Fortnite maker Epic Games, have called for Huang's reinstatement.
Musk claimed that "critical deals" involving Nvidia's technology would be lost following Huang's resignation, which has also prompted a campaign by shareholders and supporters to "Bring Jensen Back".
Huang himself has said he is open to a return, just days after resigning.

Coatsworth says he has never seen circular financing used at this scale before, but admits there are competitive rivals around, which could insulate the wider AI industry from any potential slowdown at the firm.
When Nvidia's share price plunged in the wake of the affair revelations, the stock of its rival semiconductor makers including AMD, Broadcom and Marvell Technology jumped.
"I don't think all AI activity grinds to a halt if Nvidia slows down what it's doing and if it pulls some financing, but it does change how people would look at the whole situation," Coatsworth adds.
The risk of a slowdown has already rattled stock markets. Investors took fright at Democrat gains in the midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms.
Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will actually pay off.

Investment in AI is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to investment bank Goldman Sachs, who said the technology would remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year.
Nvidia's interim boss Colette Kress said it was "business as usual" without Huang at the helm as the company's rapid growth remains on track.
The value of the shares in Big Tech companies have cushioned the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs, buoying investments and pensions for people worldwide.
Despite Huang saying he would be "honoured" to return, Nvidia's board has said it is not considering bringing him back.
And while Coatsworth thinks "no CEO is irreplaceable", he admits the pressure is on for whoever succeeds him.

articles.title: Jeff Bezos says he was 'heavily involved' in casting Robert Pattinson as new Bond
articles.standfirst: The Amazon chairman says he was originally "biased against" Pattinson "because he's already so famous".
paragraphs: This video can not be played
Watch: Jeff Bezos on involvement in casting Robert Pattinson as James Bond
Jeff Bezos has said he was "heavily involved" in casting Robert Pattinson as the new James Bond.

Speaking at an event in California, the Amazon chairman said he was originally "biased against" Pattinson - who starred in many blockbuster films like Batman and the Twilight series - "because he's already so famous".
The role of 007 has typically gone to an actor who is not as well known at the time of casting. But Bezos said in screen tests, "it was so obvious he is James Bond".

This will be the first 007 film in the official series not under the creative control of the Broccoli family, who had overseen the franchise since the first movie in 1962. Amazon purchased MGM, which co-owns the franchise, in 2022.
"There was something special about Rob", Bezos said at Semafor Silicon Valley & The World Event on Tuesday.
Pattinson was unveiled as the franchise's seventh James Bond on Monday, taking over from actor Daniel Craig. He will star in the 26th Bond movie, due to be released in 2028.
In a statement, the London-born actor said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime."
The next Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, but its title and exact release date have not yet been announced.
The announcement comes after years of intense speculation about who will take over from Craig in one of the most high-profile - and highly scrutinised - roles in entertainment.
Robert Pattinson was unveiled as the franchise's seventh James Bond on Monday
Several other actors, including Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner and Jack Lowden, were reported to be in the frame for the role as screen tests took place in recent weeks.
But Amazon MGM ultimately went with a household name, choosing a more bankable movie star who is widely seen as a safe pair of hands.
"We ran a really tight process and made the final decision on Friday," Bezos said.
There were five finalists who went through "real, old-fashioned screen tests", acting out three different scenes in full costume, with real sets and other actors, he said.

"By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing. But there was something special about Rob and his performance," Bezos added. "It was immediately un-debated. Denis [Villeneuve], the director … we all gravitated toward Rob."
The pick comes amid widespread Hollywood cuts and consolidation, with studios struggling to get people into cinemas.
Hollywood insiders have said Pattinson was viewed as a safe pick to bring audiences in, rather than taking a risk on a new actor who could grow with the franchise.

"Maybe he's boring. Maybe Hollywood would be passing up a chance to anoint a badly needed new star. But with so much at stake for everyone involved, that all makes him the obvious pick," Hollywood journalist Matthew Belloni, who predicted the pick, wrote in his newsletter.
The BBC's Regan Morris contributed to this report.

articles.title: Security flaw found in Java, world's third-largest programming language
articles.standfirst: The same tech start-up that discovered a PHP flaw used AI to uncover a critical software bug in one of the world's most popular computer language programs.
paragraphs: A tech start-up used AI to uncover a critical software bug in Java that had existed for more than a decade (generic photo)
A cyber-security firm has used artificial intelligence (AI) to uncover a critical flaw in the hugely popular computer programming language Java.
Tech start-up Calif - which recently identified a cyber-security flaw in another language, PHP - found the bug in Java's memory functions.
Java is a popular programming language used by nearly all of the world's top companies such as Apple and Amazon, as well as many banks, hospitals and governments.
It is meant to make the IT world more secure by managing your memory online, said computer scientist Professor Toby Walsh, which is why "this is such an unlikely and serious flaw".
The discovery comes after a string of serious technology issues, including a massive Microsoft outage.
On Tuesday, the US National Security Agency said its internal communications went offline on Tuesday due to a "scheduled routine maintenance".
The NSA did not specify whether its outage was linked to the identified Java bug.
Apple also reported multiple services suffered full outages due to an internal update, while a network failure grounded all flights in the US.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was "zero evidence" the incidents were related.
With the help of AI, Calif discovered a serious security vulnerability it has called Java4Shell, which allowed an adversary to remotely execute unwanted commands to Java's memory system.
In this case, the adversary was OpenAI's recently-released model GPT-6 Cyber, which is not yet available to the public.
Oracle, the owner of Java, released a "critical patch update" on Tuesday, which it said contained security vulnerability fixes - including for this flaw.
At this stage it is unclear if any platforms or companies have been affected by the latest incident.
But the Java flaw remains a huge concern for cyber-security experts, who say overloading a system's memory is one of the most common ways for hackers to exploit or crash a system.
The BBC has contacted Oracle for comment.
Nearly every critical sector, including banking, national security systems, aviation and telecommunications, relies on Java.
First released in 1995, the programming language and computing system is now the "beating heart of the modern economy", Calif said in its investigation.
One of its main functions is to manage and protect memory for you, Walsh, a leading researcher in AI, told the BBC.
Any time you transfer information on the internet, receive a file from a user or need to log into an IT system with a password, the platform you are using is likely relying on a Java program.
The serious flaw could comprise "critical financial systems, customers and organisation's data," cyber-security expert Dr Pedram Hayati said.
In Australia alone, almost every bank uses Java for managing critical transaction data, Hayati added.
The latest incidents have exposed how nearly every critical sector - including national security systems, aviation and telecommunications - relies on legacy infrastructure online.
Earlier this week, thousands of customers at major US banks, including JP Morgan Chase, Wells Fargo and Bank of America, reported trouble accessing services.
The Java discovery follows a critical cyber-security flaw identified in the PHP programming language, also identified by Calif.
PHP is the code that websites like Wikipedia use to collect information and present it in a way you can read on the web.
Surrey Centre for Cyber Security Prof Alan Woodward said the PHP flaw affected some 30 million websites, leaving them vulnerable to malicious attacks.
At the time, website owners were urged to check if their sites were affected and, if so, they were told to install updates to patch the issue or consider going offline.
The PHP flaws went undetected for at least a decade, which Walsh said is similar to what has happened with Java.
"It's been hiding in plain sight for 12 years", he said.
"AI is now exposing more flaws much more quickly," Walsh said including ones that may have been so obscure and difficult that humans could not have discovered them alone.
Earlier in November, OpenAI president Greg Brockman announced his company was pivoting 25% of its staff to focus on cyber-security demands.

Restrictions on the type of work an official can do after leaving the civil service are governed by BARs – the business appointment rules. Once administered by the advisory committee on business appointments (ACOBA), the BARs for senior (directors general and permanent secretaries) civil servants and special advisers is, as of 2025, overseen by the civil service commission, the arms-length body that regulates recruitment into the civil service.  

It is a system which, the institute has long argued, is in need of overhauling – and so a new report by the civil service commission is welcome. It sets out recommendations which will, if accepted, contribute to a more porous and expert civil service, and government should reform the BARs in line with the review recommendations. It will then need to go much further to open up the civil service. 

Business appointment rules have been harming the civil service 

While developing people and skills is crucial, part of creating an effective workforce will always mean being able to access experience and expertise from outside when it is required. Something with which the civil service has long struggled.  

There are a whole host of reasons, cultural and structural, behind that. But BARs are one part of the picture. As the Institute’s research from 2022 set out, the BARs have been acting as a disincentive for external applicants, in particular senior ones to technical roles. The rules could, in theory, restrict you from taking up work in your field of expertise for up to two years after leaving the civil service. And in process terms, even if there are ultimately no restrictions on your future employment, it might take you months to get clearance to take up that role – by which time the window may well have closed. That is very real uncertainty, and a very real disincentive for outsiders to take up a role in the civil service. It is not the only reason external experts don’t come in, but it is a factor. 

Government should act on the commission's review 

That the civil service commission, which already regulates entry, is leading this work on exits for senior officials is a good start; career shapes are shifting and the service should be encouraging – with appropriate ethical safeguards – careers that move in and out of government. The rules have not been meaningfully updated since the 1970s, and no longer reflect the reality of modern work or the skills the service needs. This review should result in a much-needed update.  

Two things are particularly welcome. First, a recognition that the current rules conflate sector expertise with improper advantage, and that this must change. The civil service needs experts, and there should be a sizeable chunk of them who are able to come into government and return to their field of expertise without being unduly punished for doing so. Second, the recognition that much of this is about culture and process efficiency, rather than only about the rules themselves. There is no point updating the rules if the myths around them still hold, or if it will still take months for officials to receive the all-clear on low-risk roles.

The government should act on the commission’s review, reforming the system so that it provides greater clarity for officials, and more proportionality. The review recommends, for example, that for fixed-term appointments of a year or less, conditions should be agreed upon before employment is taken up. As the Institute has previously argued, it should be possible, before joining a role, to see very clearly what restrictions on your activity will look like after you leave. 

Opening up the civil service will need far more than BARs reform 

These recommendations are still only one small piece of the civil service’s ongoing struggle with porosity. As the cabinet secretary said in her recent lecture, “we disincentivise our brightest talent from stepping outside the Civil Service to gain vital experience, and bringing that critical knowledge back”.  

Unblocking this problem requires a series of inter-linked initiatives. More recruitment, especially in central government departments, needs to be done externally. New talent can’t find its way in if many job adverts are still only visible to civil servants. That in turn means addressing the underlying reasons, or perceptions, that drive recruitment from the existing pool of civil servants: security vetting takes too long; onboarding is patchy; there’s no consistent training offer so new team members need to already ‘get’ government; the recruitment process favours internal candidates anyway.

The government is making good steps on some of this, including the new national school of government and public service, and the decision to scrap the ‘success profiles’ currently used to recruit. There are pockets of excellence that show it can be done differently without the system falling over, such as the recruitment exemptions in place for the AI Security Institute.  

Being able to bring in more external people while controlling the size of the civil service also requires better tools to increase the number of leavers from the civil service. A sharper practice and culture around poor performance management, and tighter workforce planning are all part of the same picture.

BARs reform is a helpful piece of the puzzle of breaking open the civil service. But it is only one part of a much bigger ambition on porosity and reform.

articles.title: Three figures we should all pay attention to in the Milburn Review
articles.standfirst:
It’s finally here: the Milburn Review of young people and work was published today. It’s big (over 250 pages); it’s bold (“a new settlement for the next generation”); and it’s brash (if its recommendations were implemented in full, it claims the UK would be “NEET Zero” by 2036-7).   There are many, many numbers in … Continued
The post Three figures we should all pay attention to in the Milburn Review appeared first on Resolution Foundation.
paragraphs: It’s finally here: the Milburn Review of young people and work was published today. It’s big (over 250 pages); it’s bold (“a new settlement for the next generation”); and it’s brash (if its recommendations were implemented in full, it claims the UK would be “NEET Zero” by 2036-7).

There are many, many numbers in the report (the best ones, naturally, are citations of Resolution Foundation research…), but just three of them taken together tell us a lot about Milburn’s recommended programme for change.

First, the report contains a dizzying array of recommendations for investment in service provision: £5.8 billion-worth in 2036-37 (in current prices). Some of this would be restitution for the austerity years (think greater further education funding); some would fund genuinely new services like a permanent youth employment scheme or support for young people with mental health problems.

That £5.8 billion of extra support sounds like a big figure, but it still likely falls short of the level of spending we observe in the lowest NEET countries. For example, Milburn’s proposed additional £3 billion for employment support for under-25s would take the UK from being a low spender on active labour market policies for young people relative to other European countries, to roughly middle of the pack.

And getting all these services and schemes working in concert, which is central to the Review’s vision, would also be no mean undertaking. This would require multiple departments and indeed multiple levels of government to work together to boost youth participation. Milburn recommends introducing a “Youth Opportunity Test” that applies to every government department, plus new duties on schools and local government, to achieve just this.

Which leads us to the second number. The Milburn Review concludes that a combination of early intervention, improved health support, more education and training investment and active labour market policies would result in a ‘big bang’ when it comes to youth employment. By 2036-37, the Review estimates 440,000 more young people would be in employment as a result, and that this would save the state £2.4 billion in 2036-37 as higher taxes and lower benefits are paid.

But achieving that outcome, too, may prove quite the task. Dividing the £5.8 billion of extra support by the 440,000 extra young people the report says will get into employment as a result suggests the average cost of getting each additional young person into work will be around £13,000. Sounds like a lot? It’s not. Past employment support schemes have spent around £30,000 per additional young person employed. Milburn’s £5.8 billion on employment, health and other support would have to be about three times as effective to get 440,000 additional young people into work.

And finally, to number three. The Review finds that the extra spending and savings resulting from the various recommendations balance out after a decade, on the basis that there are £3.6 billion of savings from “welfare reform”, a polite term for benefit cuts achieved through restricted eligibility, lower levels and/or shorter award lengths.

Make no mistake, these are the savings from cuts not from extra employment. And for those worried they are not tough enough, note that this is equivalent to half of the estimated £7.1 billion youth health and disability benefit bill in 2036-37 (in 2026-27 prices). And these reforms won’t just affect young people that are NEET: almost two-thirds of PIP recipients aged 16-24-years are in education or employment for example, many of whom could lose large amounts of support.

But alongside that (very important) debate about winners and losers, there are other radical aspects of Milburn’s vision for the benefit system. The Review recommends localising large parts of the system (a new local Health and Disability Fund, for instance); the introduction of far greater discretion and simultaneous loss of statutory entitlements for young people whose health conditions are not deemed severe or long-standing; and the creation of a separate system for young people which will mean cliff edges galore when young people turn 18 and then again when they turn 25.
A system that pays for itself should not be an end in itself

In all, then, Milburn has proposed £5.8 billion of investment, £3.6 billion of benefit cuts, and believes that after a decade, higher youth employment will also save the state £2.4 billion more. Fiscal neutrality will be achieved!

But the Review also shows the extent to which public spending has been increasingly skewed to older people over time, with the gap between spending on children and young people versus spending on pensioners widening over the past two decades. In that context, whether or not the recommendations are cost neutral is arguably the wrong test.

What the report has shown today is that moving the dial on NEETs will require wholescale change and investment across the system. As the details are debated (and the recommendations will have to make their way through a White Paper, Budget and a Spending Review next year), that may be the most important lesson we should all take from the Milburn Review.

articles.title: Northern Ireland’s “government in name only” is failing to deliver
articles.standfirst:
Northern Ireland’s “government in name only” is failing to deliver sam.macrory Tue, 17/11/2026 - 20:11 Dominant parties in Northern Ireland don't seem to pay a price for their inability to deliver better outcomes. 4 Comment Jill Rutter Institute for Government Yes Stormont is the home of the Northern Ireland Assembly and Executive, but both government and parliament need to work better in Northern Ireland. Devolution Northern Ireland protocol Sinn Féin Democratic Unionist Party Social Democratic and Labour Party Deputy first minister of Northern Ireland First minister of Northern Ireland Northern Ireland executive
No

The last Conservative government finally persuaded the DUP to re-establish the Executive in February 2024 – two years after it collapsed when the DUP withdrew over the implementation of the then Northern Ireland Protocol. Rishi Sunak had failed to persuade the DUP that the Windsor Framework was sufficient reason to return, and it took almost another year for the DUP to extract enough concessions to agree to go back in. 

Initially it looked as though relations between Sinn Féin First Minister Michelle O’Neill and deputy First Minster Emma Little-Pengelly were going well, as the new team launched with a spirit of optimism, common purpose and a willingness to get to grips with deep-seated policy problems. But initial progress has since stalled and relations have deteriorated to such an extent that the DUP are now refusing to join joint activities with the First Minister. This left Northern Ireland with no political representation at the prime minister’s recent National Economic Council with the leaders of the devolved governments. 

But a bigger problem is what Sam McBride of the Belfast Telegraph termed “government in name only” at our webinar on Northern Ireland. Decisions are not being made. The much poorer performance of the health service in Northern Ireland than in the other parts of the UK is still not being addressed, despite years of reports detailing how it needs to be rationalised. The NI Executive is rejecting the latest bail out offer from Westminster – and refuses to contemplate extra local revenue raising, preferring instead to look to UK taxpayers to underwrite them. They know the UK government usually blinks first and the moral hazard merry-go-round of failing to take tough decisions continues. 

There is a lack of accountability when voting is little affected by delivery 

In theory, Northern Ireland should have politicians capable of facing up to long-term decisions because power sharing means they face minimal electoral jeopardy. Indeed, identity voting reduces the electoral penalty for poor performance. But so far there is no evidence that the dominant parties pay a price for their inability to deliver better outcomes in Northern Ireland. 

Sinn Féin have benefited from Michelle O’Neill’s decision to stand with the citizens of the Garvaghy Road in opposition to the controversial Drumcree march, even if the DUP’s response has hamstrung the Executive. A recent LucidTalk poll put the party at an impressive 28 per cent, despite the other main nationalist party, the SDLP, being seen to have been making a good fist of Opposition. The incentives to play to the base will only increase as the next elections approach.

On the other hand, accountability may finally be catching up with the DUP, who are shedding votes to a reenergised UUP (who they displaced in the mid-2000s as the principal unionist party) on one side and to the even harder line TUV (Traditional Unionist Voice) on the other. That same poll showed the three unionist parties all in the lowish teens, with the UUP just edging ahead. Advocacy of Brexit, failure to deliver in government and the move from insurgent to party of government all seem to be catching up, and the battle over Assembly seats is hotting up for next May.

Andy Burnham’s Brexit reset should reduce the tension over the Windsor Framework

Any search for stability is also dependent on decisions in Westminster over relations wit the EU. The move for GB to dynamically align with EU sanitary and phytosanitary rules, expected to be signed off, should reduce the divergence between NI – still following most single market rules –and the rest of the UK. If Andy Burnham aims to go further when he sets out his options, the differences would diminish – though so too would any “best of both worlds” advantage. But if the Conservatives or Reform UK looked like approaching government, Northern Ireland would be forced yet again to address the consequences of a breakdown in UK-EU relations over their desire to leave the ECHR. It is far from clear any Executive could cope with those pressures. 

Northern Ireland needs its institutions to work better

The Good Friday Agreement set up institutions (with slight modifications since) designed for power-sharing arrangements, but both government and parliament need to work better in Northern Ireland. In our webinar, David Sterling, the former head of the Northern Ireland Civil Service, pointed to the possibility of the three smaller parties going into opposition when the next Executive is formed. Ann Watt explained what Pivotal, Northern Ireland’s independent policy think tank, would be looking at in their new project on possible reforms to make Stormont more effective. Andy Burnham has hinted the government is looking at that too. And Ulster University’s Deirdre Heenan asked (somewhat plaintively) what level of divergence in public service standards between different parts of the UK a responsible government in Westminster could really tolerate – a great issue to throw back at a prime minister whose big idea is devolution. 

Whatever his answer, Andy Burnham will, at least, face scrutiny for his decisions. For now, Northern Ireland’s politicians seem to keep getting away without making any.

articles.title: Milburn’s ambitious NEETs reform vision leaves difficult questions unanswered
articles.standfirst:
Milburn’s ambitious NEETs reform vision leaves difficult questions unanswered sam.macrory Tue, 17/11/2026 - 19:06 The conclusion of Alan Milburn’s review of young people Not in Education, Employment or Training (NEETs) is wide ranging and ambitious. 5 Comment Ben Paxton Institute for Government Yes Alan Milburn has provided both a clear diagnosis and a clear political vision. Public finances Welfare Spending review Health Education and skills Labour Burnham government Department for Work and Pensions
No

Alan Milburn’s highly ambitious NEETs review sets out a diagnosis of “whole system failure” and calls for a “whole system reset” solution. The recommendations run well into triple figures, and span several departments and all tiers of government. He wants an expanded, personalised and prevention-focused system of support to help young people into earning or learning, which is absolutely the right direction of travel for this broken system. 

Milburn’s review sets out important steps towards this goal, but by leaning heavily on legal guarantees of support without specifying funding for them, and not answering big questions on the shape of a new youth benefits system, difficult decisions remain on how to put this review into practice. 

A strong system of local employment support will better support young people

Milburn is right to put a new local system of support for NEETs at the heart of his proposals. Young people face multiple barriers to employment, which no single department can address. Strategic authorities are the right level for setting up a coherent, integrated system of support since they aim to reflect labour market geographies and have responsibilities for relevant policy areas, including skills and local growth (and are due to be aligned with boundaries for other relevant services in the future). 

The review proposes a ‘Youth Opportunity Service’ in every area of England by 2029. This would engage people early, and create a personalised ‘Participation Plan’ for each young person who is NEET (similar to the ‘Personalised Support Plan’ the IfG recently recommended). It would bring together services – including health, skills and employment support – and act as a single front door for both young people and employers. The review also recommends significant expansion of apprenticeships and further education provision and £1.1bn of subsidies to encourage employers to hire young people – with the Youth Opportunity Service connecting people to job opportunities and this support.

Milburn’s Youth Opportunity Service is a national model but would, crucially, be designed and delivered by strategic authorities. A ‘Participation Agreement’ would set out multi-year funding for strategic authorities, and the outcomes against which they would be held accountable. The focus on outcomes is right, but this system should work alongside the wider accountability and devolved funding model outlined in the upcoming devolution white paper – rather than try to work outside these structures.

Related content

Designing and delivering employment support

New targets and legal guarantees will not automatically lead to better support

The review proposes several new laws and statutory guarantees. The most significant of these are an ‘Opportunity Guarantee’ for every young person of a route into education, employment or training, and a ‘Support Guarantee’ of access to relevant health and employment support. Strategic authorities would be responsible for delivering these through the Youth Opportunity Service, with details of the guarantees specified in future legislation and funding as part of the ‘Participation Agreement’.  

Milburn also proposes new targets and statutory responsibilities for the health and education systems. For schools, these include more ambitious targets for school readiness at age five and work experience becoming a statutory duty. The NHS would be required to fast track access to mental health support for NEETs, alongside enforcing new maximum waiting time standards for youth mental health services. Integrated Care Boards (ICBs) would also be legally required to “work with MSAs and other local agencies to increase youth participation”, and ensure services are integrated.

Targets can help improve performance, and legal entitlements can help individuals access services and enforce minimum standards. But it matters how legal entitlements are defined, enforced and funded. Ultimately, an entitlement is only as good as the support that is actually available.

There is a risk that already stretched services are being asked to do more, without them getting the funding needed to do so. Layering responsibilities in this way can be counterproductive. It can distort wider service provision, including squeezing spend on more preventative activity to fund statutory requirements, and restrict local services rather than supporting flexible and collaborative outcomes-based working. For example, requirements already in place for ICBs and local authorities to work together on children’s social care and SEND have not successfully aligned incentives or led to better outcomes. Strong cross-agency working is more often enabled by clear outcomes and accountability, flexibility to share budgets and sustainable multi-year funding – which the Milburn review proposes elsewhere.

Related content

Performance Tracker 2025: Local government
Joining up SEND

Designing and delivering employment support

How can government better support people out of work due to ill health?

Read our report

Milburn’s benefits plan doesn’t address contentious eligibility questions    

Milburn’s review provides both a clear diagnosis of the social security system’s many problems and a clear political vision of what reform should achieve. He proposes a new separate benefits system for young people, with a new ‘Youth Allowance’ to replace Universal Credit standard and health elements, alongside a new youth disability benefits system. 

The high-level principles of Milburn’s vision are correct: a new system should better connect people to the wider range of support they need, rather than narrowly pigeon-holing them into oversimplified benefit categories. But the details of what this would mean in practice – and the fundamental but difficult questions about eligibility – remain unanswered. 

The review does not address the important and highly contentious issues of defining who should be eligible for support with ‘demonstrable extra costs’ from their disability, or who counts as ‘profoundly disabled’. Given the breadth of this review, not addressing these questions here may be reasonable. But these choices on eligibility will determine what savings these reforms are expected to deliver, which will be important for working out how the new system is funded at next year’s spending review. Proposing a new system, but leaving these questions unanswered, means the coming months will feature significant public and parliamentary debate on eligibility.  

Strong political leadership and sustained government focus are vital for success

Adults over 25 are outside the scope of this review, and the Timms review will make recommendations on disability benefits shortly. But Milburn rightly points out that the government should reform social security for all adults – a challenge which will, along with navigating the debates over the youth benefits system and then its delivery, require strong political leadership.

The attention Milburn has brought to the problems in the social security system is welcome – and he is right that this is a unique opportunity for change. 

But the ability of this impressive review to drive forward meaningful improvements will depend on government sustaining focus on improving the system, even when the difficult decisions in 2027 arrive. Having Milburn at the helm of a new Youth Opportunities Unit at the centre of government to shape and deliver the government’s response, and reporting directly to the prime minister, should give it a strong chance of success.

paragraphs: Ben Paxton welcomes the attention that Alan Milburn has brought to problems with the social security system – but says his ambitious reforms leave government facing a series of difficult decisions

Alan Milburn’s highly ambitious NEETs review sets out a diagnosis of “whole system failure” and calls for a “whole system reset” solution. The recommendations run well into triple figures, and span several departments and all tiers of government. He wants an expanded, personalised and prevention-focused system of support to help young people into earning or learning, which is absolutely the right direction of travel for this broken system.

Milburn’s review sets out important steps towards this goal, but by leaning heavily on legal guarantees of support without specifying funding for them, and not answering big questions on the shape of a new youth benefits system, difficult decisions remain on how to put this review into practice.

Milburn is right to put a new local system of support for NEETs at the heart of his proposals. Young people face multiple barriers to employment, which no single department can address. Strategic authorities are the right level for setting up a coherent, integrated system of support since they aim to reflect labour market geographies and have responsibilities for relevant policy areas, including skills and local growth (and are due to be aligned with boundaries for other relevant services in the future).

The review proposes a ‘Youth Opportunity Service’ in every area of England by 2029. This would engage people early, and create a personalised ‘Participation Plan’ for each young person who is NEET (similar to the ‘Personalised Support Plan’ the IfG recently recommended). It would bring together services – including health, skills and employment support – and act as a single front door for both young people and employers. The review also recommends significant expansion of apprenticeships and further education provision and £1.1bn of subsidies to encourage employers to hire young people – with the Youth Opportunity Service connecting people to job opportunities and this support.

Milburn’s Youth Opportunity Service is a national model but would, crucially, be designed and delivered by strategic authorities. A ‘Participation Agreement’ would set out multi-year funding for strategic authorities, and the outcomes against which they would be held accountable. The focus on outcomes is right, but this system should work alongside the wider accountability and devolved funding model outlined in the upcoming devolution white paper – rather than try to work outside these structures.

The review proposes several new laws and statutory guarantees. The most significant of these are an ‘Opportunity Guarantee’ for every young person of a route into education, employment or training, and a ‘Support Guarantee’ of access to relevant health and employment support. Strategic authorities would be responsible for delivering these through the Youth Opportunity Service, with details of the guarantees specified in future legislation and funding as part of the ‘Participation Agreement’.

Milburn also proposes new targets and statutory responsibilities for the health and education systems. For schools, these include more ambitious targets for school readiness at age five and work experience becoming a statutory duty. The NHS would be required to fast track access to mental health support for NEETs, alongside enforcing new maximum waiting time standards for youth mental health services. Integrated Care Boards (ICBs) would also be legally required to “work with MSAs and other local agencies to increase youth participation”, and ensure services are integrated.

Targets can help improve performance, and legal entitlements can help individuals access services and enforce minimum standards. But it matters how legal entitlements are defined, enforced and funded. Ultimately, an entitlement is only as good as the support that is actually available.

There is a risk that already stretched services are being asked to do more, without them getting the funding needed to do so. Layering responsibilities in this way can be counterproductive. It can distort wider service provision, including squeezing spend on more preventative activity to fund statutory requirements, and restrict local services rather than supporting flexible and collaborative outcomes-based working. For example, requirements already in place for ICBs and local authorities to work together on children’s social care and SEND have not successfully aligned incentives or led to better outcomes. Strong cross-agency working is more often enabled by clear outcomes and accountability, flexibility to share budgets and sustainable multi-year funding – which the Milburn review proposes elsewhere.
How can government better support people out of work due to ill health?

Milburn’s review provides both a clear diagnosis of the social security system’s many problems and a clear political vision of what reform should achieve. He proposes a new separate benefits system for young people, with a new ‘Youth Allowance’ to replace Universal Credit standard and health elements, alongside a new youth disability benefits system.

The high-level principles of Milburn’s vision are correct: a new system should better connect people to the wider range of support they need, rather than narrowly pigeon-holing them into oversimplified benefit categories. But the details of what this would mean in practice – and the fundamental but difficult questions about eligibility – remain unanswered.

The review does not address the important and highly contentious issues of defining who should be eligible for support with ‘demonstrable extra costs’ from their disability, or who counts as ‘profoundly disabled’. Given the breadth of this review, not addressing these questions here may be reasonable. But these choices on eligibility will determine what savings these reforms are expected to deliver, which will be important for working out how the new system is funded at next year’s spending review. Proposing a new system, but leaving these questions unanswered, means the coming months will feature significant public and parliamentary debate on eligibility.

Adults over 25 are outside the scope of this review, and the Timms review will make recommendations on disability benefits shortly. But Milburn rightly points out that the government should reform social security for all adults – a challenge which will, along with navigating the debates over the youth benefits system and then its delivery, require strong political leadership.
The attention Milburn has brought to the problems in the social security system is welcome – and he is right that this is a unique opportunity for change.

But the ability of this impressive review to drive forward meaningful improvements will depend on government sustaining focus on improving the system, even when the difficult decisions in 2027 arrive. Having Milburn at the helm of a new Youth Opportunities Unit at the centre of government to shape and deliver the government’s response, and reporting directly to the prime minister, should give it a strong chance of success.

articles.title: Government 2027: IfG's annual conference
articles.standfirst:
Government 2027: IfG's annual conference Muirin.Keating Tue, 17/11/2026 - 08:42 Burnham government Online event Number 10 Number 10 North Wednesday 13 January 2027, 06:00
Government reform Civil service reform Local government Public sector Artificial intelligence Labour Institute for Government Wednesday 13 January 2027, 09:00 GMT Civil service Ministers Public bodies Public finances Public services Regulation Policy making Parliament and the constitution The IfG will bring together influential speakers and experts to explore the key questions for government in 2027.

Government 2027, the Institute for Government’s flagship annual conference, will bring together influential speakers, front-bench politicians, policy makers, opinion formers and experts to explore the key questions facing Andy Burnham’s government – and opposition parties – in the year ahead.

This year’s conference will also mark the launch of the IfG’s new strategy and new mission statement: How to make government work well for the people of the UK. In a packed day of keynote speeches, panel discussions, new polling and in-conversation events, Government 2027 will explore the government’s devolution agenda, its plans for rewiring the state, the opportunities and threats of AI, what can be done to restore trust in political leaders and more.

Our panel events include:

What does the polling say?  

What do the public want to see most from government – and are these changes that Andy Burnham, or another political leader, can deliver?  

Brand-new polling, conducted in partnership with More in Common, will set the scene for the government in 2027.
 

Legitimate and resilient institutions: How can the civil service be rewired for 21st century government?

While each government has its own priorities, it is the civil service that is responsible for delivering them.  

Our expert panel will discuss how the civil service can be made more legitimate and more resilient to political changes in an increasingly fragmented landscape.
 

Politics and policy in the age of AI: How can government grip the technological revolution?  

Gripping the potential of AI could be key to making the government machine more efficient and effective. But can the government keep up with the rapid pace of technological change while also managing the risks?

This panel will explore how to best embed better use of AI in government while maintaining high levels of accountability and expertise.
 

The devolution revolution: Will Andy Burnham’s power giveaway succeed?    

Andy Burnham has put English devolution at the heart of his agenda – but what will decentralised government really look like?  

Our panel will explore which powers should be devolved, how mayors and locally-elected politicians can best work with central government, and the role of No.10 North in delivering the PM’s ambitions.
 

A crisis of trust: What can be done to restore faith in political leaders?  

Governments across the world have seen a sharp decline in trust in politics and politicians. So what can be done to turn around the public’s view?

Our final panel will discuss what skills are needed from our political leaders – and the promises and policies set up by governments – if trust is to be rebuilt.
 

We would like to thank Grant Thornton UK LLP for supporting this event.

articles.title: US Bifurcation, aging, and job growth are shaping the metro consumer outlook
articles.standfirst: Although AI-related investment has been a major driver of US growth over the past year, consumer spending remains the backbone of the economy. Identifying which households, spending categories, and locations are powering spending is crucial to pinpointing opportunities for B2C companies.
paragraphs: Household spending power has become more concentrated over time

Although AI-related investment has been a major driver of US growth over the past year, consumer spending remains the backbone of the economy. Identifying which households, spending categories, and locations are powering spending is crucial to pinpointing opportunities for B2C companies.

Spending has become more reliant on high-income, asset-rich households, buoyed by equity and housing wealth, while lower-income households have struggled. This bifurcation has likely been heightened by the inflation shock from the US-Israel war with Iran and will continue to influence spending going forward.

Another trend that will shape spending is the aging of the population. As seniors gradually take up a greater share of the population, where they live and what they buy will matter more for spending growth.

Although high-income metros (e.g., San Jose) and retiree hotspots (e.g., The Villages) feature toward the top of our medium-term spending growth rankings, many of the top performers are still those with the strongest job growth prospects (e.g., Austin), most of which are located in the Sun Belt. By contrast, several Northeast and Midwest metros are forecast to lag, hindered by sluggish employment and population prospects, and in some cases, exposure to the spike in the price of essentials.

Slower-growing but large metros should not be dismissed as offering limited opportunities. The sheer size of cities like Chicago means that lower growth rates can still translate into huge spending level gains.
We expect discretionary categories (e.g., recreation and culture) and health to record the fastest growth over the medium term, supported by high-income households and seniors, respectively.

articles.title: London’s safeguarded wharves demand and capacity research
articles.standfirst: Commissioned by the Greater London Authority, this Oxford Economics research forecasts the wharf capacity London will need to 2050. It finds a potential shortfall, with construction materials demand alone exceeding capacity by 622,000 tonnes, and shows that where capacity sits matters as much as how much
paragraphs: London’s safeguarded wharves play a vital role in keeping the capital supplied with the materials and goods it needs, while helping to take freight off congested roads and reduce transport emissions. But with pressure growing to release riverside land for housing and other development, how much wharf capacity will London need in the decades ahead? Commissioned by the Greater London Authority (GLA), this research by Oxford Economics examines the freight handled by London’s safeguarded wharves, identifies the factors driving future demand and forecasts the capacity required to 2050.

Drawing on ten years of freight data from the Port of London Authority, forecasts of industrial demand and interviews with wharf operators, the research provides a detailed picture of how the market could evolve. It examines seven commodity groups, from construction materials and agricultural bulks to metals, petroleum products and waste, and considers how demand will vary across the North East, South East and West regions of the Thames. The findings point to a potential capacity shortfall by 2050, with demand for construction materials alone forecast to exceed available capacity by 622,000 tonnes. The analysis also highlights important differences between regions, suggesting that the location of future capacity could be just as important as its overall level.

The findings have important implications for the future of London’s riverside infrastructure and its ambitions for growth. They highlight the need to consider not just how much wharf capacity the capital requires, but where it is located, which commodities it can handle and how efficiently it is used. The report also explores the uncertainties surrounding future demand and capacity, including the impact of major infrastructure projects, wharf closures and changing river connectivity. Together, the analysis provides an evidence base to inform decisions about the future safeguarding of London’s wharves and the role of the Thames in supporting a growing, more sustainable city.

Andy Logan leads our Consultancy offer on different industries for clients. He undertakes studies forecasting the demand for company’s products, analysing the drivers of different industries growth, and assessing the size of different markets and industries. He also investigates the competitive pressures and opportunities facing industries now and in the future. Another area, where he has a keen interest is in studies assessing the demand and supply of labour for different industries and occupations, identifying potential skill shortages and implications for migration.
He has worked with clients in most industries, and in many countries of the world.

Prior to joining Oxford Economics, Andy worked in a variety of economist roles at the Bank of England for 15 years. His research focused on the labour market, commodity and producer prices, UK trade flows, and the performance of UK banks. He holds an MSc. and BA. degrees from the universities of London and Leicester.

Emily is a Senior Economist on the Industry team where she supports bespoke industry projects in areas such as renewable energy, construction and insurance. She is also involved in other projects like economic impact studies.

Prior to joining Oxford Economics, Emily worked for 5 years as a government economist for the UK Civil Service, working in the Department for International Trade (DIT) and the Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy (BEIS). In DIT she worked on assessing the socio-economic impact of Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) and Freeports. She also worked in a crisis covid-19 analytical team, providing supply chain analysis and reporting of critical goods to ministers. In BEIS, she used economic analysis to develop policy positions for manufactured goods for both Free Trade Agreements, the Northern Ireland Protocol and the UK's Global Tariff Schedule. Emily holds a Bsc in Economics from the University of St Andrews.

articles.title: The Economic Importance of Motorcycles to Europe
articles.standfirst: In 2024, motorcycle-related activity supported €35.1 billion in GDP, 481,600 jobs and €20.6 billion in tax revenues across the EU and the UK. This study shows how manufacturing, sales, repairs and events ripple through supply chains, and how trade barriers and competition shape Europe’s global position. It also models how more motorcycle commuting could cut travel time, costs and CO₂ emissions.
paragraphs: A Report for the European Association of Motorcycle Manufacturers (ACEM)

In 2024, motorcycle-related activity supported an estimated €35.1 billion in GDP, 481,600 jobs and €20.6 billion in tax revenues across the EU and the UK. These figures capture the sector’s own operations, its supply chains and the wider spending it supports, including spending by employees and visitors attending motorcycle events.

The analysis covers motorcycle manufacturing, sales and repairs, as well as accessories, sports and promotional events. Drawing on official statistics, industry data and economic modelling, it traces how these activities support businesses across the economy. For every €1 of GDP generated directly by the sector, a further €2.30 was supported elsewhere.

International trade is another important part of the picture. Around half of EU motorcycle and parts production was exported in 2024. The report examines Europe’s position in global markets and how trade barriers, growing competition and regulatory complexity affect the industry’s opportunities to invest and expand.

The study also explores how motorcycle use can reduce commuting times, operating costs, emissions and demand for urban space. Around 6.4 million people across the EU and the UK already commute by motorcycle. Under a modelled scenario in which 5% of car commuters switched to motorcycles, the report estimates potential annual savings of 28 million days of commuting time and 2.6 million tonnes of CO₂. It also considers how motorcycles can complement public transport and other modes within urban mobility plans.
Associate Director of Economic Consulting, Continental Europe

Stefan Gorgels is Associate Director for economic consulting services in Continental Europe, focusing on economic impact analysis and econometric analysis. He has a strong academic background in economics and extensive experience in managing consulting and research projects for national and international clients.

Prior to joining Oxford Economics, Stefan was a manager at DIW Econ - the consulting arm of the German Institute for Economic Research - where he managed economic consulting and research projects for a wide range of clients, including companies, industry associations, German government ministries and the European Commission.
Stefan Gorgels holds a B.Sc. in Economics from Maastricht University, an M.Sc. in Economics from the Barcelona Graduate School of Economics and a Ph.D. in Economics from New York University.

Before joining Oxford Economics in 2025, Johanna worked at DIW Econ, the consultancy firm of the German Institute for Economic Research. During her time there, Johanna led several high-profile projects assessing the economic impact of different industries and institutions, as well as projects addressing socioeconomic and environmental issues. Johanna holds an M.Sc. in Economics and Management from Leibniz University Hannover.
