articles.title: Concrete’s role in meeting housing and infrastructure demand to 2050
articles.standfirst: Our new research for the Global Cement and Concrete Association (GCCA) explores how global megatrends are reshaping infrastructure demand and highlights the critical role of cement and concrete in supporting economic development, improving living standards and building a more sustainable future.
paragraphs: Our new research for the Global Cement and Concrete Association (GCCA) explores how global megatrends are reshaping infrastructure demand and highlights the critical role of cement and concrete in supporting economic development, improving living standards and building a more sustainable future.
The world is entering a period of unprecedented demand for infrastructure and housing.

Our latest research forecasts that global construction activity will increase by more than 70% by 2050, reaching US$16.6 trillion annually, up from US$9.7 trillion in 2025. Emerging economies across Asia, Africa and the Middle East will be major engines of growth. Delivering these assets will create substantial opportunities across the construction industry.

However, infrastructure need does not automatically nor quickly translate into funded projects. Capacity constraints and financing pressures can slow delivery, while expanding materials supply requires capital and long lead times. This creates a difficult investment decision: committing too early risks underused capacity, while waiting too long can mean supply is unable to respond when projects proceed.

For investors, infrastructure owners and policymakers alike, this means that understanding when and where this growth will occur, and the barriers to delivering it, is essential to planning ahead and capturing the opportunity.
The report identifies five interconnected forces that are driving the next generation of infrastructure investment.

The practical implication is that companies need to understand which sectors will expand, how quickly projects can proceed and whether their capabilities match the work coming through. Policymakers and asset owners need to anticipate where competing demands will stretch delivery capacity.
Cement and concrete sit at the centre of this outlook. Concrete’s durability, scalability and local availability make it essential to delivering the infrastructure underpinning modern economies.

Our research estimates that annual concrete demand from key infrastructure sectors will reach around 20 billion tonnes by 2050, demonstrating the scale of future opportunities for construction materials producers and suppliers. Transport sectors (roads, and rail and ports) stand out with faster demand growth than other sectors. Nevertheless, the utilities sector remains a large source of demand in absolute terms.

The report also highlights the important contributions the cement and concrete industry make beyond its physical applications. Importantly, these include its contributions to regional economic development and industrial capacity, as well as its crucial role in supporting the transition to a lower-carbon economy through resilience and whole-life asset performance.

The outlook presents a substantial opportunity, but meeting infrastructure needs will require more than expanding production. As the report details, growing infrastructure investment will need to meet increasingly demanding expectations for affordability, resilience and sustainability.

Innovation in materials, construction methods and circular economy practices will be essential in improving delivery. Clearer and more credible project pipelines and procurement arrangements can give suppliers greater confidence to invest. The opportunity is to deliver more infrastructure and economic value per tonne of concrete, per unit of carbon and per worker.

Understanding where demand is emerging, what could constrain delivery and how requirements are changing will help organisations make better decisions about the capacity, capabilities and assets needed over the coming decades.

The full Oxford Economics report exploring the global megatrends, economic evidence and strategic implications for infrastructure investment and the cement and concrete industry is available here. For the wider construction market outlook, explore our subscription-based Global Construction Service. For bespoke research tailored to your business needs, fill in the form on this page to contact our expert team.
Head of Construction & Infrastructure Consulting, OE Australia

Adrian has over 23 years of economic analysis and consulting experience with Oxford Economics Australia, focusing on the infrastructure, building, maintenance and mining industries. Adrian has undertaken a wide range of consultancy projects for the public and private sector based on his detailed understanding of construction, mining and maintenance markets, their drivers and outlooks, the range of organisations operating in this space and the issues they face.

This work includes deeper industry liaison, contractor and competitive analysis, pipeline analysis, demand and cost escalation forecasting, and industry capacity and capability projects for the public and private sector. He is the lead author of major reports but also undertakes briefings and workshops for senior management, board members and industry associations, leads in-depth stakeholder consultation, and facilitates and chairs roundtables between government and industry.

Ryan is a Senior Economist currently responsible for supporting the production of the Asian Construction Service. He has experience in econometric modelling and consulting and holds a Bachelor's degree in Commerce and Economics (Honours), majoring in econometrics and finance.

articles.title: Washington Can Start Delivering on Affordability by Rejecting Trump’s Tariffs
articles.standfirst: This new Congress will need to address the existing policies hurting affordability, prepare for Social Security insolvency in 2032, and build a regulatory environment that allows American dynamism to flourish.
paragraphs: Voters in the last two election cycles have clearly shown that they care about the cost of living. In response to the inflationInflation is when the general price of goods and services increases across the economy, reducing the purchasing power of a currency and the value of certain assets. The same paycheck covers less goods, services, and bills. It is sometimes referred to as a “hidden tax,” as it leaves taxpayers less well-off due to higher costs and “bracket creep,” while increasing the government’s spendin following the COVID-19 pandemic, voters handed the Democratic party a significant setback and put Republicans in charge of the House, Senate, and White House. And, after two years of decisions from Washington that have driven up prices at the gas pump, the grocery store, and the assembly line, voters have again rejected unaffordable policies.

Indeed, polling from August revealed that Americans want their costs to fall more than they want additional handouts or carveouts through the taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. code. By a 20-point margin, respondents said they want the government to focus more on lowering costs rather than boosting wages.

Newly elected members of the House and the Senate shouldn’t ignore them. But next year, with the looming debt ceiling expiration and Democrats’ long list of spending priorities, they’ll be tempted to return to a tax and spend agenda. If history is any indication, it just won’t deliver the affordability Americans desire.

articles.title: IRS Filing Data Show Higher Refunds and More Itemizers Following OBBBA
articles.standfirst: New IRS data for tax year 2025 shows how tax refunds and taxes owed at filing time changed under the new tax breaks enacted as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA).
paragraphs: New IRS data for taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. year 2025 shows how tax refunds and taxes owed at filing time changed under the new tax breaks enacted as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA).

The OBBBA changed several provisions of the individual income taxAn individual income tax (or personal income tax) is levied on the wages, salaries, investments, or other forms of income an individual or household earns. The U.S. imposes a progressive income tax where rates increase with income. The Federal Income Tax was established in 1913 with the ratification of the 16th Amendment. Though barely 100 years old, individual income taxes are the largest source code, but some of the largest changes for tax year 2025 were the creation of several deductions: for tip income, overtime, senior citizens, and auto-loan interest paid. The standard deductionThe standard deduction reduces a taxpayer’s taxable income by a set amount determined by the government. Taxpayers who take the standard deduction cannot also itemize their deductions; it serves as an alternative. was larger ($15,750 for single filers and $31,500 for joint), as was the child tax creditA tax credit is a provision that reduces a taxpayer’s final tax bill, dollar-for-dollar. A tax credit differs from deductions and exemptions, which reduce taxable income rather than the taxpayer’s tax bill directly. (up $2,200 per child), and the itemized deductionItemized deductions allow individuals to subtract designated expenses from their taxable income and can be claimed in lieu of the standard deduction. Itemized deductions include those for state and local taxes, charitable contributions, and mortgage interest. An estimated 13.7 percent of filers itemized in 2019, most being high-income taxpayers. for state and local taxes paid (SALT, which was increased from $10,000 to $40,000).

Unfortunately, the data update does not provide any new information on the new OBBBA provisions. While we can analyze how refunds and taxes due at filing time changed across filers, we cannot analyze the uptake or usage of the new provisions themselves.

Most of the tax relief from the new OBBBA changes occurred during the filing season, as taxpayers either owed less to the IRS than they would have paid otherwise, or received larger refunds. We can compare this year’s filing season data, which covers through July 30, 2026, to last year’s filing season data through the same week, to analyze how the filing seasons changed.

The total amount of tax owed at filing time fell by 8 percent year over year, while the number of taxpayers owing a balance dropped more sharply by 21.3 percent. For tax year 2024, 40.6 million returns paid nearly $236 billion at filing time. For tax year 2025, far fewer returns, 31.9 million, paid a lower $216 billion at filing time.

While taxes owed went down, tax refunds went up, growing nearly 21 percent year over year. In tax year 2024, 100 million tax returns received $329 billion back from overpayments, and that rose to 109.6 million tax returns receiving nearly $397 billion back from overpayments for tax year 2025. The average refund size increased by $328 from $3,290 in tax year 2024 to $3,617 in tax year 2025.

The biggest percentage decrease in taxes owed at filing was experienced by filers making between $50,000 to $100,000 (falling 23.1 percent year over year), while the biggest percentage increase in total refunds received was experienced by filers making between $200,000 to $500,000 (rising 54.6 percent year over year).

Last filing season, 132.9 million filers took the standard deduction (90.9 percent) compared to nearly 12.7 million who itemized (8.7 percent). This filing season, more taxpayers itemized. About 130.7 million filers took the standard deduction (88.6 percent) while 16.2 million itemized (11.0 percent).

This 27.9-percent increase in itemization is a predictable consequence of one of OBBBA’s biggest individual tax changes for tax year 2025: the increase in the state and local tax (SALT) deductionThe state and local tax (SALT) deduction permits taxpayers who itemize when filing federal taxes to deduct certain taxes paid to state and local governments. The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) capped it at $10,000 per year, consisting of property taxes plus state income or sales taxes, but not both. cap.

Taxpayers claimed $253.3 billion in SALT deductions through mid-July, compared to just $96.3 billion in deductions at the same point for tax year 2024 filings. Taxpayers with adjusted gross incomeFor individuals, gross income is the total of all income received from any source before taxes or deductions. It includes wages, salaries, tips, interest, dividends, capital gains, rental income, alimony, pensions, and other forms of income. For businesses, gross income (or gross profit) is the sum of total receipts or sales minus the cost of goods sold (COGS)—the direct costs of producing goods (AGI) between $200,000 and $500,000 increased SALT claims the most relative to last year. OBBBA increased the SALT cap from $10,000 to $40,000 for tax year 2025, but the higher SALT cap phases out for taxpayers earning more than $500,000.

The IRS data through July 30, 2026, provide no new information on claims for the “no tax on” provisions from OBBBA: the deductions for tips, overtime, auto loan interest, and the enhanced senior deduction.

The Treasury Department published a press release in June 2026 with limited data on how many taxpayers claimed the new deductions and the average deduction size. The IRS filing season data are more granular and allow researchers to examine total deductions claimed by AGI cohort.

Absent a filing season update, policymakers, researchers, and the public may have to wait until annual IRS Statistics of Income (SOI) data are released for tax year 2025 for more data on the “no tax on” provisions. Given IRS data lags, those data may not be published until 2028—the year these temporary provisions are scheduled to expire.

While we know that the OBBBA delivered tax relief for individual taxpayers—as millions fewer taxpayers owed at filing time and refunds were up—we still lack detailed data on how filers utilized the new provisions.

articles.title: Forecasting The Future Of Forecasting
articles.standfirst: Can AI forecast the economy better than models we already have? That depends. In one comparison for near-term UK CPI, a simple linear model has proven hard to beat, as...
paragraphs: NIESR and the University of Birmingham recently hosted a workshop on Economic Forecasting with AI. With presentations of five papers and a round table discussion, we learned how LLMs and other machine learning methods are potentially pushing the boundaries of macroeconomic forecasting. But a key question remains: what do we value more, accuracy or the mechanisms behind our forecasts? In this Monday Interview, Senior Economist Peter Dixon asks Associate Economist Charlotte O’Leary which methods are being applied, what AI is capable of and where the limitations lie.

That depends. In one comparison for near-term UK CPI, a simple linear model has proven hard to beat, as past inflation plus seasonality carries most of the signal. Our participants explained that this is because inflation is endogenous: when central banks see pressure building, they act, so the pressure never fully shows up, leaving inflation best predicted by its own past. Furthermore, data is scarce: monthly figures provide only a few hundred observations; even using CPI sub-components does not come anywhere near generating the millions of observations that methods like neural networks (NNs) require, so their extra flexibility tends to fit noise.

LLM forecasts, on the other hand, are nearly perfect. Or so they would seem. One of the presenters stripped the dates, series name and country from their dataset, and found that the LLM beat linear forecasts in almost every horizon. This, however, stems from a contamination problem. The LLM was able to name the exact quarter on two-thirds of occasions, and within one year 98.8 per cent of the time. When explicitly told to disregard all prior knowledge of the economy, the only thing that changed was its verbal compliance, its behaviour, did not. Hence, for now, out-of-sample testing is very limited.

Three places stood out. The first is measurement. Claude Opus 5 coded 56 years of Federal Reserve Beige Books, around 6,400 reports, into a usable time series in under one day for roughly $300 (~£225). Added to a standard real-time recession model, this text index managed to date business-cycle turning points more accurately, cutting the average timing error from about three months to under two.

The second is scenario analysis. A multi-recurrent neural network trained on UK data produced policy responses that depended on the state of the economy. The same combination of monetary easing had an estimated effect on GDP some four to five times larger in late 2008 than in 2015. The model also identified significant interactions between interest-rate and liquidity shocks, suggesting that their combined effects cannot simply be inferred by adding their individual impacts. Interestingly, the results also point to the importance of broad money in explaining economic developments during periods of financial stress. This resonates with the literature on Divisia monetary aggregates, which suggests that appropriately weighted measures of money can provide useful information about exchange-rate movements, particularly when conventional interest-rate indicators become less informative.

A third area of interest is simulation. Bank of England researchers used an LLM to create synthetic respondents to the Inflation Attitudes Survey. These matched average perceptions during the 2022-23 spike and offer a cheap laboratory for testing communication and survey design.

Discipline. Results need contamination testing, to ensure a clear separation between training, validation and test data. Moreover, researchers need to be open about the software frameworks, model specifications and implementation choices since these can give materially different results. In one paper, for example, the same Long Short-Term Memory neural network architecture gave noticeably different forecast errors when run using the Python frameworks TensorFlow and PyTorch. Reproducibility is a serious concern when using stochastic models, and when vendors change their default LLMs without notice this can seriously impact on the results. One participant noted that such a switch resulted in a loss of access to the temperature setting that their method relied on. One potential thing that could help is using locally hosted models with known training cut-offs and testing their forecasts only on the periods that follow.

This brings us back to the issue of accuracy versus mechanisms. For policymakers, the most accurate model is not necessarily the most useful as they need to know why a forecast has changed and what happens if policy changes. It is here that AI still falls short. The neural network’s scenarios are not structurally identified, and LLMs are even further removed from a structural model.

The consensus was, therefore, that the future is hybrid. Machine learning is good at finding nonlinear patterns, which are particularly helpful for events like the GFC, whereas econometrics and structural models impose causal discipline, where human judgement plays a role in interpreting the results. AI thus makes economics more important, not less. One member set out the challenge clearly: AI will have truly advanced when it can explain the reasoning behind its forecasts and produce credible conditional scenarios. We are not there yet.

articles.title: US PCE nowcast – Broadening pressures lock in December rate hike
articles.standfirst: Our nowcast is for headline PCE inflation to rise to 3.8% y/y in October, up from 3.6% y/y in September. The details suggest high energy prices are lifting food inflation and bleeding into core inflation. This will be discomforting to the Federal Reserve and bolster our expectation for a 25bp rate hike at the December Federal Open Market Committee meeting; we think markets are overpricing the odds of a 50bp hike.
paragraphs: Our monthly PCE nowcast provides an early estimate of inflation trends ahead of official data releases, highlighting key drivers and implications for Federal Reserve policy.

Our nowcast is for headline PCE inflation to rise to 3.8% y/y in October, up from 3.6% y/y in September. The details suggest high energy prices are lifting food inflation and bleeding into core inflation. This will be discomforting to the Federal Reserve and bolster our expectation for a 25bp rate hike at the December Federal Open Market Committee meeting; we think markets are overpricing the odds of a 50bp hike.

Recent declines in oil prices bode well for our forecast for headline inflation to peak in Q4, and the pass-through from higher energy prices to core inflation will ease over 2027. Muted equity markets, lower demand for homebuying, and modest wage growth should keep services inflation benign.

Each month, we replicate the Bureau of Economic Analysis’ (BEA) methodology to estimate the PCE deflator using the source data from the CPI, the PPI, and import prices. Because some underlying data and seasonal adjustments aren’t publicly available, there’s a small tracking error. Our average absolute errors since we began this approach are 3bps for headline and core PCE. Almost all the errors are in the core services ex-housing category, where the share of confidential data is the largest.

articles.title: Not All Bipartisan Tax Ideas Are Created Equal
articles.standfirst: Unfortunately, not all bipartisan efforts will make for sound tax reform. Both parties have leaned into the “no tax on” trend in recent years, complicating the tax code and narrowing the US income tax base.
paragraphs: The midterm election results mean that Washington is heading towards another era of divided government, with Democrats controlling both chambers of Congress and a Republican still in charge at the White House. While the two parties have plenty of disagreements over taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities., trade, and fiscal policy, there are areas where they might agree and compromise in 2027 and 2028.

Some of these areas could represent meaningful progress on sound tax policy, such as enhancing full expensingFull expensing allows businesses to immediately deduct the full cost of certain investments in new or improved technology, equipment, or buildings. It alleviates a bias in the tax code and incentivizes companies to invest more, which, in the long run, raises worker productivity, boosts wages, and creates more jobs. for multifamily housing construction or improving taxpayer services at the IRS. Congress could also pursue a bipartisan opportunity to roll back some of the economically harmful tariffs the Trump administration has imposed in recent years—or, better yet, reclaim its legislative authority over trade and tariffTariffs are taxes imposed by one country on goods imported from another country. Tariffs are trade barriers that raise prices, reduce available quantities of goods and services for US businesses and consumers, and create an economic burden on foreign exporters. policy.

Unfortunately, not all bipartisan efforts will make for sound tax reform. Both parties have leaned into the “no tax on” trend in recent years, complicating the tax code and narrowing the US income tax baseThe tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates.. Lawmakers are also considering new or revived carveouts for specific sectors of the economy, including the film and television industry and clean energy companies.
Below, we review the tax policy items—good and bad—that may attract bipartisan support in next year’s new Congress.

While Republicans have controlled both chambers of Congress and the White House for the past two years, lawmakers in both parties have been hard at work on several bipartisan priorities. Several bills may merit consideration during the “lame duck” session in November and December 2026, including:
In the new session of Congress, beginning on January 3, 2027, lawmakers may have several additional opportunities for bipartisan tax reform:

Several tax ideas have emerged with bipartisan support that would make the tax code more complicated, cost needed revenue, or provide targeted tax carveouts that distort economic activity at the expense of other taxpayers.

The new Congress may have several opportunities to change direction on tax, trade, and fiscal policy over the next two years. Bipartisan cooperation will be the key to unlocking any number of reforms in divided government.

But not all bipartisan tax policy is created equal. Lawmakers should keep the principles for sound tax reform—simplicity, neutrality, transparency, and stability—central when considering new tax policies in 2027.

articles.title: Bank Taxes in Europe, 2026
articles.standfirst: 13 European OECD countries have implemented financial stability contributions (FSCs), commonly referred to as “bank taxes.” Explore the 2026 data.
paragraphs: The 2007-2008 financial crisis triggered a global debate on whether—and, if so, how— taxation can be used to stabilize the financial sector and generate revenue to partially cover the costs associated with financial crises. The issue has returned to the spotlight since 2023, as banks have benefited from higher interest rates and governments have sought new sources of revenue in the wake of the 2022-23 inflationInflation is when the general price of goods and services increases across the economy, reducing the purchasing power of a currency and the value of certain assets. The same paycheck covers less goods, services, and bills. It is sometimes referred to as a “hidden tax,” as it leaves taxpayers less well-off due to higher costs and “bracket creep,” while increasing the government’s spendin shock.
Following the financial crisis and the more recent inflation surge, policymakers and international organizations have explored several approaches:
Today’s map shows which European countries implemented financial stability contributions (FSCs), commonly referred to as “bank taxes.”

Austria, Belgium, Cyprus, France, Greece, Hungary, Iceland, the Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Slovenia, Sweden, and the United Kingdom all levy bank taxes. Almost all of these countries implemented the levy following the 2007-2008 financial crisis, with Greece (1975) the only exception.

Most countries levy their bank taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. on a measure of liabilities or a measure of assets. However, some countries decided on a different tax baseThe tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates.. For example, France taxes the minimum amount of capital necessary to comply with the regulatory requirements.

While bank taxes raise relatively little revenue, they can reduce the sector’s capacity to support lending, investment, and economic activity. Over time, they may also reduce the amount of available capital, limiting banks’ ability to absorb losses and respond to unforeseen financial crises.

articles.title: Portland’s Proposed Fair Share Tax Yields Astronomical Tax Burdens
articles.standfirst: As Portland City Council considers the proposed tax increase, they should understand the city’s starting point—as arguably the highest-tax jurisdiction in the entire country—not one of the lowest.
paragraphs: Under the Fair Share Tax, a proposal pending before Portland City Council, some corporations could soon face a 26.2 percent state and local income taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. rate, plus a 1.57 percent gross receipts taxGross receipts taxes are applied to a company’s gross sales, without deductions for a firm’s business expenses, like compensation, costs of goods sold, and overhead costs. Unlike a sales tax, a gross receipts tax is assessed on businesses and applies to transactions at every stage of the production process, leading to tax pyramiding. rate (not accounting for a partial deduction for the cost of labor or cost of goods sold, which will vary by business). For a business with a 7 percent profit margin, that represents a 48.6 percent rate on net income just from state and local income and gross receipts taxes, before even considering federal taxes or local property taxes. But one of the proposal’s co-sponsors, City Councilor Mitch Green (D-District 4), argues the proposed tax shouldn’t be a concern because, he contends, Portland’s current business taxes aren’t actually high.

The Councilor’s proposal would add a multiplier to the existing city business license (income) tax with rates based on CEO compensation ratios, with the highest rate set at 15.6 percent—higher than the highest state corporate income taxA corporate income tax (CIT) is levied by federal and state governments on business profits. Many companies are not subject to the CIT because they are taxed as pass-through businesses, with income reportable under the individual income tax. of 11.5 percent in New Jersey. This would be in addition to Oregon’s 7.6 percent top state corporate income tax rate, a 2 percent county tax, a 1 percent regional tax, and both city and state gross receipts taxes.

Councilor Green contends that Portland’s current business tax burdens are reasonable and specifically objects to our prior analysis, which finds that Portland has some of the highest business taxes in the country. But can his claim be true? Is it possible that, as his office purports to show, Portland’s business taxes are almost 40 percent lower than Pittsburgh’s and barely a quarter of Seattle’s?

The answer is, of course, no: Portland is a uniquely high-tax jurisdiction, and the calculations the Councilor relies on are deeply flawed. The results raise obvious red flags, such as the fact that the calculations for Seattle yield a 142 percent effective tax rate for a typical business from sales, payroll, and gross receipts taxes alone. Even without considering federal income taxes, local property taxes, or any other taxes, Councilor Green’s comparative tables show a Seattle business paying the entirety of its profits, and then 42 percent more, in state and local taxes. Seattle’s taxes are high, but they aren’t that high.

It’s worth understanding how these calculations went awry, because correcting the errors yields precisely the conclusion that the so-called Fair Share Tax’s sponsor attempts to disprove: Portland’s business taxes are already uniquely high.

Both Portland and the state of Oregon have gross receipts taxes, which are major drivers of the region’s high business tax burdens, though a constellation of state, regional, county, and city income taxes also contribute significantly to the overall tax bill. Oregon does not, however, levy a sales taxA sales tax is levied on retail sales of goods and services and, ideally, should apply to all final consumption with few exemptions. Many governments exempt goods like groceries; base broadening, such as including groceries, could keep rates lower. A sales tax should exempt business-to-business transactions which, when taxed, cause tax pyramiding. —one of five states to forgo one. The Councilor’s analysis attempts an “apples-to-apples” comparison by converting other jurisdictions’ taxes into gross receipts tax equivalents, but errs in several respects, nowhere more significantly than in the conversion of general sales taxes into gross receipts tax equivalents.

The Councilor’s FAQ recognizes that sales tax calculations drive the results but fails to recognize that the calculations are gravely in error. After a table comparing Portland to several other jurisdictions, the text reads: “Notice that Portland’s various tax rates sum to a fairly large number, just under Seattle’s. But after converting to the equivalent tax on gross receipts, these rates become very small. Indeed, because Oregon and the jurisdictions therein do not have a sales tax, the actual tax burden is much lower than other cities.”

In Seattle, for instance, sales taxes are estimated to cost businesses 5.93 percent of gross revenue, which is almost 85 percent of the income of a business with 7 percent profit margins. Seattle’s sales taxes alone are estimated to impose as much as 243 percent of the total business tax burden calculated for Portland (2.44 to 2.54 percent of gross revenue), which is clearly mistaken.

The Councilor’s analysis converts sales tax rates into gross receipts equivalents by dividing the general sales tax rate by 1.78 percent, based on a misinterpretation of a paper that estimates 1.78 as the ratio of gross receipts to final consumption. The paper’s estimate is entirely reasonable and is essentially identical to the ratio of US gross output to GDP. It is a ratio of all transactions to consumption and has nothing to do with sales taxes.

Total consumption is not the same as taxable sales. It includes transactions largely excluded from sales tax bases (like healthcare, insurance, groceries, and legal services), and it even includes consumption that does not involve a transaction, like the imputed value of living in one’s own home. And while some business-to-business transactions are taxed, and their costs are at least partially borne by businesses, it’s also clearly mistaken to apply all the cost of sales taxes—a consumer tax—to businesses.

The magnitude of this error can be demonstrated by applying the Councilor’s methodology to sales taxes nationwide. That yields $2.37 trillion in business sales tax burdens in FY 2024, whereas total state and local sales tax collections were about $588 billion, including both consumer and business purchases.

To put this in further context, EY and the Council on State Taxation estimate that businesses paid about $245 billion that year, one-tenth of what Councilor Green’s methodology suggests. Federal corporate income tax collections were $472 billion in FY 2024, making the Councilor’s estimates of businesses’ share of state and local sales tax burdens five times what the federal government collects in corporate income tax revenue.

In other words, the primary reason Portland’s taxes look modest compared with other jurisdictions is that the analysis takes the one major tax Oregon lacks and overstates its burdens by a factor of ten.

The comparison also contains other errors and omissions. It applies Seattle’s Social Housing Tax, which applies only to compensation above $1 million per employee, and its JumpStart Housing Tax, which applies only to larger businesses, to all wages. It lists Pennsylvania’s corporate income tax but drops it from Pittsburgh’s total tax calculation, omits California’s corporate income tax entirely, excludes Oregon’s TriMet employer payroll taxA payroll tax is a tax paid on the wages and salaries of employees to finance social insurance programs like Social Security, Medicare, and unemployment insurance. Payroll taxes are social insurance taxes that comprise 24.8 percent of combined federal, state, and local government revenue, the second largest source of that combined tax revenue., applies Portland’s Clean Energy Surcharge to all businesses, and disregards deductions under the Oregon CAT. These errors cut both ways, but they indicate a haphazard approach. Property taxes (on real property as well as machinery and equipment), which represent about 34 percent of all state and local taxes paid by businesses, are also omitted, though this omission is acknowledged.

The Councilor’s own analysis yields a 36.3 percent effective rate on a business with 7 percent profit margins from state and local business income and gross receipts taxes alone, even before the new tax, which is astonishingly high. It’s too high, in fact, due to several calculation errors. But the reality is that Portland’s taxes are very high, and the Councilor’s analysis does nothing to contradict that. It merely compares it favorably to vastly inflated rates in other jurisdictions.
These are not just calculation errors. They also flow through into the broader analysis.

The Councilor’s FAQ argues, for instance, that low-margin businesses like grocery store chains will be able to handle an increased tax burden in Portland since the increase is supposedly minuscule compared to “the actual sales taxes in Vancouver, Washington, where there are plenty of grocery stores despite state and local taxes 45 times higher than this ordinance proposes.” Not only does this rely on the previously mentioned miscalculation of sales tax burdens, converting an 8.9 percent sales tax into a 5 percent tax on grocers’ gross receipts—an impossible 250 percent effective rate from sales tax alone, based on the Councilor’s correct identification of grocery store profit margins as about 2 percent—but it misses the fact that Washington, like most states, exempts groceries from the sales tax.

Portland already has anomalously high business taxes, and the proposed tax would make those rates astronomical. Business taxes imposed based on sales into a jurisdiction tend to show up in prices, meaning Portland consumers would bear a substantial share of the increased tax burden, even if large corporations are the ones to remit the tax. Some businesses may find that they can no longer afford to operate in Portland at all, reducing consumer choice and undercutting local employment.
As Portland City Council considers the proposed tax increase, they should understand the city’s starting point—as arguably the highest-tax jurisdiction in the entire country—not one of the lowest.

Jared Walczak is a Senior Fellow at the Tax Foundation, where he spent five years as Vice President of State Projects, and president of Walczak Policy Consulting.

articles.title: Are We In The ‘Foothills’ Of AI-Driven Growth?
articles.standfirst: It seems we finally have some good economic news to cheer about. GDP grew by 0.7 per cent in Q3, making the UK the second-fastest-growing economy in the G7, behind...
paragraphs: It seems we finally have some good economic news to cheer about. GDP grew by 0.7 per cent in Q3, making the UK the second-fastest-growing economy in the G7, behind only the US. This was the fastest quarterly growth since the end of 2017 excluding the post-pandemic recovery (although growth at this rate was normal before the pandemic). So, in this post we dig into whether we are seeing the start of an AI-driven growth boom as some in government have claimed, drawing out the implications for the labour market and interest rates as well as the broader economy.

The first place to look for the effect of AI is in the investment needed for its infrastructure. Spending on data centres, servers, semiconductors, connections to the power grid, and the software itself should show up as a boost to investment. In that context, it’s encouraging that investment has been strong in recent quarters – contributing around half of GDP growth in Q3. More compellingly, if we look at the assets that are being invested in – as shown in Figure 1 – it’s ICT equipment and buildings where investment is concentrated. So this picture is at least consistent with a growth bump from AI investment, albeit this is very much circumstantial evidence. It’s also important to stress that the contribution to UK GDP will depend on the extent to which this new infrastructure is imported, and how much is produced at home and in that context, it’s striking that net trade was a drag on GDP in the latest data. This is something that we should expect to continue.

More importantly for a service-based economy like the UK’s, it is AI adoption across knowledge-intensive business services that will start to drive process improvement which will show up in the GDP statistics as higher value added in these sectors. By automating routine tasks, improving research and analytical capabilities, and enabling firms to deliver more output with fewer labour inputs, AI should raise productivity. (As an aside, there are also big measurement challenges around capturing AI – so we should take the latest data with a pinch of salt (for more on this see the 2026 Deane-Stone lecture from the ONS’s James Benford on measuring the effects of AI). In this context, while significant differences in AI adoption remain across sectors, uptake has been on an upward trajectory over the past three years (Figure 2). If the link between AI usage and output growth persists, continued expansion across firms points to more broad-based economic gains in the future.

So, what can the data tell us about the benefits of adopting AI? Again, we don’t have direct evidence, but the signs are good. As Figure 3 shows, the latest pick up in output has come with a boost from growth among a group of industries that are likely to be providing AI services (a definition coined by the Bank of England). Growth in sectors likely to adopt AI – including financial and business services – has also picked up sharply through the course of this year. Together, these sectors account for around three-fifths of the pick up in growth through the course of this year.

Note: AI services encompass SIC 58, SIC 62, and SIC 63, following the Bank of England November 2026 Monetary Policy Report. Early adopters are SIC sections J (excluding AI services), K, and M. Public services are SIC sections O, P, and Q. Source: ONS, NIESR calculations

To be clear, this does not quantify the contribution of AI to growth; rather, it shows that the sectors driving growth this year are precisely those where one would expect AI-related gains to show up first.

Seeing early signs of AI-related activity is particularly encouraging given that there are good reasons to think such gains should emerge slowly. Any company starting to use a new technology may initially see productivity fall given time taken to understand how to use the technology and, for example, make the complementary investments required to realise its potential. This includes significant complementary investments in intangible capital, including redesigning processes, training workers, restructuring the organisation and developing new products and approaches. This means AI may actively reduce measured output and productivity in the near term. But, as firms exploit the technology the gains should become apparent. Academic work for the US that digs into this AI J-curve finds that unmeasured intangible investment associated with computer hardware and software raises so-called total factor productivity. As Robert Solow put it during the ICT boom of the 1990s: “you can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics”

To put some flesh on the bones of our AI-related inferences, we can look to the ONS Business Insights and Conditions Survey, which has tracked AI adoption across firms since late-2023. Unsurprisingly, the ICT sector leads the pack with 60 per cent of firms confirming their use of AI in the latest vintage, up from 30 per cent in the first. Professional services follow in second place, at two-fifths of firms. At the other end of the scale, fewer than 20 per cent of firms in the hospitality and construction sectors report AI usage. Figure 4 shows that differences in adoption have broadly mapped onto output growth over the past year: not only have AI-intensive sectors led growth, but year-on-year declines in output have been concentrated in sectors with fewer than one in five firms using AI.
Source: Business Insights and Conditions Survey, NIESR calculations

The first thing to say here is that there is a lot more of this to come. One way to look at this is to ask: how far does the AI infrastructure buildout still have to run? A recent Brookings paper tackles this head on, finding that around 57 GW of US data-centre capacity was in place by the middle of this year compared with a pipeline of more than 500 GW. Such estimate should be taken with a healthy pinch of salt – not least because there are good reasons to doubt that all of this capacity will ultimately come on stream. Nonetheless this estimate makes clear that – even in the US – we might only be a tenth of the way through the buildout currently envisaged. To put this in perspective, the work estimates that to deliver this would mean investment of nearly 4 per cent of US GDP in the coming years – way more than was spent during periods of previous general purpose technology rollouts, for example during the railroad, electrification, highway and telecommunications booms.

As we show in simulations from NIESR’s global econometric model NiGEM, published in our recent Economic Outlook, such a scenario is not all good news for the UK, however. There are gains in the form of exports to the US. But, as already mentioned, we are not big players in the data-centre supply chains, so these effects are modest. More importantly, they are likely to come with chunky increases in longer-term interest rates as demand for investment capital globally spirals. Indeed, as set out in our recent Market Anatomy, around a third of the rise in gilt yields since February seems likely to be attributed to the rise in demand from AI investment. If we are only a tenth of the way through the buildout, there will be more upward pressure on interest rates, tightening financial conditions and dampening UK economic activity. An implication of this is that the Chancellor should certainly not bank on a fall in the cost of borrowing providing a substantial boost to the public finances in the near future.

The other potential dark cloud to the silver lining of AI-driven growth could come from the labour market. The context here is the warning issued this week from central banks that AI – among other factors – is leading to lower labour demand, putting downward pressure on hiring. Figure 5 provides some extra evidence here, showing that around one in ten businesses expect AI to reduce their headcount in the future, roughly double the 6 per cent already reporting AI-related reductions. By contrast, only 2 per cent anticipate a positive impact. In short, if we are in the foothills of AI-driven growth, then we are likely also at the very beginning of the labour market churn that comes with it.
Note: Figure refers to all businesses excluding those with 0-9 employed. Source: Business Insights and Conditions Survey, NIESR calculations

It’s become widely accepted that the UK is in a rut when it comes to growth. And there is a broad political consensus that this is the key policy challenge we face. Recent data do not change that fact and writing a blog about 0.7 per cent quarterly growth should itself provide a reality check about the position we find ourselves in. Nonetheless, the casual nihilism about our growth prospects should at least be tempered by these tentative signs that new technology can deliver growth. Nurturing these green shoots should certainly be a priority for policymakers – this is definitely not the moment to declare victory. But we must also think hard about what AI-driven growth comes with. If we are moving into a future of higher interest rates and rising unemployment, the challenge is not just to avoid choking off the ‘green shoots’ of growth, it is also how we learn to live with what the growth of the future comes with.

articles.title: You’ve got mail (finally): your Milburn cram sheet inside
articles.standfirst:
Afternoon all, If you’re reading this then we have survived not only doomsday but also an email free Friday – hope you enjoyed it. And avoiding the end of the world is not the only forecast to be improved upon this week. GDP grew 0.7 per cent in Q3, putting our year-to-date growth second in … Continued
The post You’ve got mail (finally): your Milburn cram sheet inside appeared first on Resolution Foundation.
paragraphs: If you’re reading this then we have survived not only doomsday but also an email free Friday – hope you enjoyed it.

And avoiding the end of the world is not the only forecast to be improved upon this week. GDP grew 0.7 per cent in Q3, putting our year-to-date growth second in the G7, behind only the US. Sadly, household incomes aren’t following – while real GDP per person has grown by 2.6% over the past two years, real household disposable income per person has been essentially flat.

Next week, there’ll be only one story in town as the Milburn review’s final report drops. Our mini-Milburn special has reads on young people’s experiences of work, a cheat sheet to help you cram, and a Chart of the Week showing how the UK’s balance between benefits and employment support stacks up against our OECD neighbours.

Plus – know an audio-visual whizz looking for a public policy role? We’re hiring a maternity cover Communications Manager who would (among other things) have the joy of working with me on our High Resolution podcast. Do share if you know a good candidate.

Catch-22-year-olds. In the last year, more than half of young jobseekers heard nothing back from any of their job applications. Have employers given up on the young? Not according to this Reed survey of 2,000 UK firms: 73 per cent say hiring early-career talent is a high priority. Nonetheless, there’s concern there about the skills and qualities they think young people are lacking: understanding the working environment (34 per cent), communication (33 per cent) and reliability (32 per cent). This brings us back to the age old ‘experience paradox’, where young people need experience to get a job, but a job to get experience. Employers’ preferred fix is (record scratch, freeze frame) a tax cut. 72 per cent say scrapping employer NICs for under-25s would boost hiring. Scroll to Something for the weekend to find out what a more cost-effective measure would look like.

Mental maths. Economics research on mental health has ballooned, and this sweeping review takes stock. The costs are large: stress, depression and anxiety accounted for 55 per cent of UK working days lost to work-related ill health in 2024-25, and research from Denmark found that people diagnosed with depression, bipolar disorder or schizophrenia earn 31 to 73 per cent less than their siblings. But the authors argue rising caseloads don’t necessarily mean worsening mental health: UK survey data show distress among 16-19 year olds edging up only modestly since 2008 (from 9 to 11 out of 36 for boys), far less than diagnoses suggest. But that view is contested. Peter Fonagy’s review for the Government found the rise in common mental disorders among English adults (from 16 to 23 per cent since 1993) “cannot be explained by greater awareness alone”. Either way, economic shocks take a real toll. In Brazil, parental job loss raised children’s chances of mental health diagnosis by 6 percentage points. Support helps: in New York, guaranteeing legal representation to families facing eviction cut new mental health diagnoses among children by 7 per cent.

Parent trap? Making people spend time applying for jobs is a huge part of the Universal Credit system – but does work search conditionality actually get people into work? New research from our friends at the IFS assesses the Lone Parent Obligation in search of an answer. Between 2008 and 2012, the age of youngest child at which single parents had to look for work was cut from 16 to five. Employment rose by 4.4 percentage points – although the typical job paid just £8,000 a year, yielding little tax. Meanwhile, disability benefit claims rose, and among children already struggling at school, GCSE results fell and absence rose. Almost 90 per cent of the gross saving disappeared, as the cuts incurred other fiscal costs in the form of alternative benefits and lower future tax payments. So conditionality got some additional parents into work, but the savings were much smaller than expected and there were downsides for the kids.

Remote control. Next week’s focus may be young people, but remote working could be part of the answer to boosting employment for other groups. Treating the pandemic jump in UK home working as a natural experiment, this blog compares occupations where it took off with those where it didn’t, and finds a boost to the employment rates of older and physically disabled workers. Each one-point rise in home working lifted full-time employment by nearly 1 per cent for disabled workers and 0.4 per cent for 50-64-year-olds. Home working explained roughly three-quarters of the rise in full-time disabled employment. Given we need to boost the employment rates of old and young, we should be cautious about rowing back from all of the pandemic flexibilities. Might need outlook to work though…
The long-awaited Milburn review lands next week – here’s key facts for you ahead of the publication (more on our Substack):

Alan Milburn wants you to know that for every £1 spent on employment support (training, job search help, wage subsidies) for young people, £25 is spent on their benefits. His review will aim to shift that balance and it looks like he’ll suggest doing so by both cutting benefits and increasing employment support. But how do other countries compare? For Chart of the week, we’ve plotted benefit spending (the x axis) against spending on employment support (the y axis) as a proportion of GDP across OECD countries. Important caveat: to get internationally comparable data we look at all ages here, not just young people. If you’re in the bottom left quadrant, you’re not spending a lot (hello America), but anyone in the top right quadrant is a big spender on both fronts (hello Denmark). The coloured lines show you where different ratios sit: if you’re on the green line (and only a handful of countries – including Sweden, Denmark and Korea – exceed it) then you’re spending five times as much on benefits as on employment support. The latest available UK data puts us comfortably on the red line meaning we spend twenty times as much on benefits as we do on employment support. It is low employment support spending, rather than high benefit spending, that is causing our high ratio. Hopefully the balance of Alan’s recommendations will reflect that.

articles.title: How to improve the ministerial submissions system
articles.standfirst:
How to improve the ministerial submissions system melissa.ittoo Fri, 13/11/2026 - 11:48 1 Report Jack Burrows-Worlidge Institute for Government No Civil service Ministers Civil servants Private office team
how-to-improve-ministerial-submissions-system
No

How ministers make decisions matters. But the submissions system – their primary mechanism for doing so – is outdated and dysfunctional.

Current practices produce mountains of paperwork and waste inordinate amounts of officials’ and a ministers’ time. The standard submission format is inflexible, resulting in advice which is poorly tailored to the issue at hand. This all makes it harder for ministers to make well-informed decisions.

This report digs inside this system, examining its processes, strengths and weaknesses, and how it can be reformed.

Not all of the proposals are new, and indeed some will be familiar to ministers and private office officials. But in discussing both best practice and more creative options, this report sets out how the submissions system can improve. This includes:

  • Making delegations clearer
  • Improving commissioning
  • Shaking up the research and drafting stages
  • Streamlining processes
  • Modernising private office systems and practices
  • Supplementing written submissions where necessary

None of these changes would replace the submissions system. Written advice to ministers, and a written record of decisions, remain vital. But even simple improvements – and more consistent application of best practice – will improve the system and support minister to make better-informed decisions.

How to improve the ministerial submissions system

articles.title: The economic impact of the UK’s beer and pub industry
articles.standfirst: An economic impact assessment of the beer and pub industry across the UK, capturing the separate impact of the breweries, pubs, off-trade and the rest of the on-trade sectors.
paragraphs: The beer and pub industry plays an important role within the UK economy both culturally and economically.

We completed an economic impact assessment of the beer and pub industry across the UK, capturing the separate impact of the breweries, pubs, off-trade and the rest of the on-trade sectors. The approach isolated the industry’s total impacts across the UK at both local authority and parliamentary constituency levels. We also completed Scottish and Welsh reports as part of this, with the latter translated into Welsh.

The beer and pub industry plays an important role within the UK economy both culturally and economically. Pubs are at the heart of many local communities, spread across the length and breadth of the country. Yet the total footprint of the industry is greater than just pubs, as it also considers the brewing of beer, as well as the sales of beer throughout hotels, restaurants, sports clubs, and in the retail trade. The beer and pub industry, therefore, has a footprint in every local community across the country.

To understand the current scale of its economic footprint in the UK economy, the British Beer and Pub Association (BBPA) commissioned Oxford Economics to update our economic impact analysis of the industry. These estimates consider the impacts from four subsectors of beer and pub activity. These are the brewing of beer, the activity of pubs, the proportion of activity in the rest of the on-trade (excluding pubs) that is attributable to the sale of beer, and the share of the off-trade that is dependent on beer sales.

articles.title: The strategic role of the EU fuel manufacturing and refining sector
articles.standfirst: Our report explores the industry’s strategic importance to the EU, the role it can play in enabling industrial transformation, and the economic risks that could emerge if refining capacity contracts faster than the transition can be delivered.
paragraphs: The EU fuel manufacturing and refining industry remains a strategic pillar of Europe’s economy and industrial base.

Our report explores the industry’s strategic importance to the EU, the role it can play in enabling industrial transformation, and the economic risks that could emerge if refining capacity contracts faster than the transition can be delivered.

In 2025, the sector supported €200 billion in GDP, 1.8 million jobs, and €83 billion in tax revenues across the EU, while supplying the fuels and feedstocks that underpin transport, manufacturing, petrochemicals, agriculture, and household activity. However, the analysis also highlights the risks of a continued decline in refining capacity. A faster-than-expected contraction could reduce EU GDP by almost €25 billion, eliminate around 120,000 jobs, lower government revenues by €14 billion, and increase the EU’s reliance on imported fuels by 2035, with implications for competitiveness, energy security, and the transition to low-carbon fuels.

articles.title: Shabana Mahmood’s immigration plans have been badly handled from the start
articles.standfirst:
Shabana Mahmood’s immigration plans have been badly handled from the start melissa.ittoo Thu, 12/11/2026 - 11:59 Complex changes to policy need cross-government buy-in and cooperation. 5 Comment Shaina Sangha Institute for Government Yes Policy making Immigration Complex policy problems Labour Home secretary Burnham government Home Office
No

Answering to a different prime minister, and dealing with a different set of cabinet colleagues, Shabana Mahmood set out her plans for immigration reform at the start of the year. The home secretary said that many migrants (including care workers) would need to wait a minimum of 10 (often 15) years to apply for Indefinite Leave to Remain (ILR). She also proposed that migrants who have arrived in the UK since 2021 – but have not yet received ILR – would be subject to retrospective changes in settlement policy. This would mean their wait for ILR status would be extended, even though the rules when they arrived in the UK set out a five-year timeline.1 Sangha S, Shabana Mahmood’s retrospective action on immigration could undermine trust in government, Institute for Government, 21 May 2026, www.instituteforgovernment.org.uk/comment/shabana-mahmoods-retrospective-immigration-trust-government

The announcement faced fierce opposition both from the sector and within the Labour Party.2 Elgot J and Osuh C, Home secretary to make some migrants wait 10 years or more for right to settle in UK, The Guardian, 1 November 2026, www.theguardian.com/politics/2026/nov/01/home-secretary-shabana-mahmood-immigration-leave-to-remain-windrush  Retrospective action is procedurally normal in certain types of policy making (for example, tax), but changes in the same category as those Mahmood proposed are far rarer and more controversial, creating heightened legal risk for government because they affect family life, employment and legal security  – as we wrote at the time.

Whether she agreed with her critics or not, Mahmood has rewritten her plans – but still ended up in a position which will still anger many, while also failing to remove the potential for legal jeopardy.

Mahmood’s new immigration policy could create big problems for the Home Office

Mahmood’s first announcement was at least built on a clear ambition. She wanted fewer people to settle in the UK (or at least take longer to do so), particularly those care workers and their dependants who had arrived post-pandemic under the Health and Care Worker visa route and who the Home Office worried would quickly become a net fiscal cost to the state. The Home Office also probably anticipated that some care workers would choose to leave the UK, therefore helping the government demonstrate progress on its ambition to reduce net migration.3 The rationalisation for this policy has changed over time, though. Facing backlash, the Home Office’s argument became that delaying settlement for care workers, in particular, will help to keep them in the sector – if they received settled status they would be able to leave their current jobs. It is a difficult tightrope to walk given that the prime minister and other cabinet ministers have expressed concern about the impact of the proposals on care workers, specifically.Mason R and Weaver M, ‘Shabana Mahmood urged to “read the room” on Labour opposition to immigration policy’, The Guardian, 21 October 2026, www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026/oct/21/cabinet-split-shabana-mahmood-immigration-plans-labour-miatta-fahnbulleh McKelvie G, ‘Angela Rayner stands by attack on care worker visa reforms ahead of Labour conference’, The Guardian, 26 September 2026, www.theguardian.com/politics/2026/sep/26/angela-rayner-care-worker-visa-reforms-labour-conferenceStavrou A, ‘Fahnbulleh turns down chance to back home secretary’s migration reforms’, The Independent, 21 October 2026, www.independent.co.uk/bulletin/news/miatta-fahnbulleh-mahmood-immigration-plans-b3070584.html

Mahmood still intends to move away from a five-year pathway to settlement (“indefinite leave to remain”, ILR) for the majority of migrants who arrive to the UK. Instead, the right to settle will be “earned”,4 Home Office and The Rt Hon Shabana Mahmood MP, Home Secretary unveils new rules for migrants settling in the UK, GOV.UK, 2 November 2026, www.gov.uk/government/news/home-secretary-unveils-new-rules-for-migrants-settling-in-the-uk  with those on salaries over £50k or in healthcare and education roles still able to apply for ILR after five years.

For all others, the default will become a 10-year wait, with new ways to shorten or extend this timeline. The adapted rules for care workers now provide a five-year route to settlement for those already in the UK so long as they have earned over £25,000 per year. Those who fall beneath this threshold will be able to apply for another five-year visa and get another shot at meeting the criteria for ILR, while those in other occupations who are ‘skilled’, like engineers and chefs, but who are earning less than £50,000, will also see their timeline for settlement extended.

Mahmood argues that these revised plans will reduce met migration, but they will still pile risk onto her department, leave the hundreds of thousands affected in limbo, and look unlikely to generate the fiscal savings promised.5 Mahmood concedes immigration overhaul savings will fall short of £10bn estimate, ITV News, 3 November 2026, www.itv.com/news/2026-11-03/mahmood-concedes-immigration-overhaul-savings-will-fall-short-of-10bn-estimate , 6 Ross A, Shabana Mahmood's savings through new immigration rules branded 'nonsense', The Independent, 2 November 2026, www.independent.co.uk/bulletin/news/shabana-mahmood-new-immigration-rules-nonsense-b3077685.html , 7 BBC News, Mahmood refuses to put cost on care worker settlement climbdown, 3 November 2026, www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm75pgqdyzldo , 8 IPPR, Skilled migrants set to boost UK public finances by £115 billion, new IPPR analysis reveals, 2 November 2026, www.ippr.org/media-office/skilled-migrants-set-to-boost-uk-public-finances-by-115-billion-new-ippr-analysis-reveals  This policy concession will penalise skilled workers, the CBI argues, “without addressing the problem the policy was originally designed to solve”.9 The CBI said the exemption for some care workers meant the policy risked “being higher costs for the relatively small number of businesses using skilled worker visas, without addressing the problem the policy was originally designed to solve”. www.cbi.org.uk/media-centre/articles/cbi-responds-to-government-changes-to-indefinite-leave-to-remain-rules/; www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026/nov/02/shabana-mahmood-softens-immigration-plans-cabinet-backlash-leave-to-remain

Related content

Shabana Mahmood’s retrospective action on immigration could undermine trust in government

Shabana Mahmood’s retrospective action on immigration could undermine trust in government

The home secretary’s immigration reforms could put her on collision course with the courts.

Read the comment

Unclear policy intention and poor policy process made Mahmood’s rethink inevitable

Reviewing policy, following challenges and considering evidence, is the right thing for ministers to do. But bold announcements, big headlines, and reversals of the kind overseen by Mahmood risk undermining trust in the system and making the UK a less desirable destination for the most valuable migrants.

As the Institute set out in Better Policy Making (2022), policy design often falls down as a result of short-termism, poor cross-government working, and Whitehall parochialism – and, unfortunately, all appear to have featured in this case.

It would have been clear to the home secretary a year ago, as it was to onlookers, that net migration was already plummeting and that creating a policy with the purpose of delaying settlement for care workers would create opposition in the sector and among the public. But Mahmood’s ambition to drive down net migration led her to pursue sweeping changes to the settlement system, with little precedent and without buy-in from the cabinet or Labour backbenches.

This relates, too, to poor cross-government working and Whitehall parochialism. The Home Office did not appear to have consulted with other departments (whose workforce strategies are highly contingent on immigration policy), much less the vast array of stakeholders that would be affected by these changes.1 Home Office, A Fairer Pathway to Settlement: Government Response to the Consultation, November 2026, https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6ae90b0e5b14ba0182a272a4/A_Fairer_Pathway_to_Settlement_-_Government_response_to_the_consultation.pdf

If Mahmood does pursue these reforms, effective implementation is essential

Mahmood appears to have internalised some criticism from colleagues and from the sector, but Better Policy Making also identifies poor implementation as the final pitfall in the road to policy success. If the government is committed to this course of action, it must ensure that implementation is excellent or otherwise risk serious policy failure.2 Evening Standard, 'Another Windrush': Labour MP sounds alarm over Mahmood's new immigration rules, 2 November 2026, www.standard.co.uk/news/politics/shabana-mahmood-immigration-windrush-dianne-abbott-b1303310.html , 3 Elgot J and Osuh C, Home secretary to make some migrants wait 10 years or more for right to settle in UK, The Guardian, 1 November 2026, www.theguardian.com/politics/2026/nov/01/home-secretary-shabana-mahmood-immigration-leave-to-remain-windrush

The home secretary’s proposals will further complicate an already opaque immigration and asylum system, which is full of financial, legal and procedural hurdles for migrants, and which is highly vulnerable to human error. Implementation is her next challenge, and she must make sure that the Home Office consults properly with those in delivery, inside the Home Office, within Border Force and at UKVI, to ensure that plans are deliverable and that training and guidance is high quality. Otherwise, an approach, and a process, which has been flawed from the outset risks unravelling all together.
